你是翻译 Agent。
用户输入是一个翻译 batch，各字段含义如下：
- sources：本批需要翻译的原文列表；
- glossary_terms：翻译时应遵守的术语及固定译法；
- style：目标译文的风格要求；
- context：当前文本之前的局部上下文；
- book_synopsis：全书主题、背景和主线概览；
- chapter_digest：截至当前 batch 之前已经确认的累计章节梗概。

你的基本任务是翻译 sources 中的全部原文。输出译文是与 sources 等长的列表，按下标对应。
翻译时结合并遵守其他输入字段提供的信息。

{
  "sources": [
    "# Late Socialism: An Eternal State",
    "Mimicry is a very bad concept, since it relies on binary logic to describe phenomena of an entirely dif­ erent nature. The crocodile does not reproduce a tree trunk, any more than the chameleon reproduces the colors of its surroundings. The Pink Panther imitates nothing, it reproduces nothing, it paints the world its color, pink on pink.",
    "—Gilles Deleuze and Felix Guattari, A Thousand Plateaus: Capitalism and Schizophrenia",
    "## An Eternal State",
    "“It had never even occurred to me that in the Soviet Union anything could ever change. Let alone that it could disappear. No one expected it. Neither children, nor adults. There was a complete impression that everything was forever.” So spoke Andrei Makarevich, the famous songwriter and musician,2 in a televised interview (1994). In his published memoirs, Makarevich later remembered that he, like millions of Soviet citizens, had always felt that he lived in an eternal state (vechnoe gosudarstvo) (2002, 14). It was not until around 1986 and 1987, when reforms of perestroika (reconstruction) were already afoot, that the possibility of the socialist system not lasting forever even entered his mind. Many others have described a similar experience of the profound feeling of the Soviet system’s permanence and immutability, and the complete unexpectedness of its collapse. And yet, Makarevich and many Soviet people also quickly discovered another peculiar fact: despite the seeming abruptness of the collapse, they found themselves prepared for it. A peculiar paradox became apparent in those years: although the system’s collapse had been unimaginable before it began, it appeared unsurprising when it happened.",
    "When the policies of perestroika and glasnost’ (openness, public discussion) were introduced in 1985, most people did not anticipate that any radical changes would follow. These campaigns were thought to be no dif­ erent from the endless stateorchestrated campaigns before them: campaigns that came and went, while life went on as usual. However, within a year or two the realization that something unimaginable was taking place began to dawn on the Soviet people. Many speak of having experienced a sudden “break of consciousness” (perelom soznania) and “stunning shock” (sil’neishii shok) quickly followed by excitement and readiness to participate in the transformation. Although different people experienced that moment differently, the type of experience they describe is similar, and many remember it vividly.",
    "Tonya, a school teacher born in Leningrad in 1966, describes the moment she first realized, around 1987, that “something impossible” (chto-to nevozmozhnoe) was taking place: “I was reading on the metro and suddenly experienced an uter shock. I remember that moment very well. . . . I was reading Lev",
    "Razgon’s story ‘Uninvented’ (Nepridumannoe),3 just published in Iunost’ [the literary journal Youth]. I could never have imagined that anything even remotely comparable would be published. After that the stream of publications became overwhelming.” Inna (born in Leningrad in 1958)4 remembers her own “first moment of surprise” (pervyi moment udivleniia), which also occurred around 1987 and 1988: “For me perestroika began with the first publication in Ogonek5 of a few poems by [Nikolai] Gumilev,” a poet of the Akmeist circle whose poetry had not been published in the Soviet Union since the 1920s.6 Inna had already read the poetry in handwriten copies but had never expected it to appear in state publications. It was not the poems that surprised her but their appearance in the press.",
    "The stream of new publications began to rise exponentially, and the practice of reading everything, exchanging texts with friends, and discussing what one had read soon became a national obsession. Between 1987 and 1988, the circulation of most newspapers and literary journals jumped astronomically, as much as tenfold and more in the course of one year.7 Often it was impossible to find many of the more popular publications at newsstands because of the speed at which they sold out. In leters to the weekly magazine Ogonek, readers complained of having to stand in line at a local kiosk at 5 a.m., two hours before it opened, to have any chance of buying the magazine. Like everyone else, Tonya tried to read as much as possible: “My friend Katia and I started subscribing to monthly literary journals (tosltye zhurnaly): Oktiabr’, Nash Sovremennik, Novyi Mir, Znamia, Iunost’. Everyone tried to subscribe to dif­ erent journals so they could exchange them with friends and have access to more materials. Everyone around us was doing this. I spent the whole year incessantly reading these publications.”",
    "Reading journals, watching live television broadcasts, and talking to friends who were doing the same quickly produced new language, topics, comparisons, metaphors, and ideas, ultimately leading to a profound change of discourse and consciousness. As a result of this process, in the late 1980s, there was a widespread realization that the state socialism which had seemed so eternal might in fact be coming to an end. Italian literary scholar Vitorio Strada, who spent much time in the Soviet Union before the transformation began, summarized the experience of the fast-forwarded history that he encountered among the Soviet people in the late 1980s: “[N]o one, or almost no one, could imagine that the collapse . . . would happen so soon and so fast. . . . The timing of the end and the way in which it occurred were simply startling” (Strada 1998, 13).",
    "The abrupt change was also quite exciting. Tonya, who had always felt proud of being a Soviet person and never identified with the dissidents, unexpectedly found herself quickly engrossed in the new critical discourse and, in her words, “felt elated” that most people were doing it—“this was all so sudden and unexpected and it completely overtook me.” Tonya remembers reading",
    "Evgeniia Ginzburg’s Steep Route (Krutoi marshrut),8 then Solzhenitsyn, then Vasilii Grossman.9 Grossman was the first to imply that Communism could be a form of fascism. This had never occurred to me before. He did not say this openly but simply compared the tortures in the two systems. I remember reading it lying on the sofa in my room and experiencing an intense feeling of a revolution happening all around me. It was stunning. I had a break of consciousness (perelom soznania). Then came the books of Vladimir Voinovich. I shared everything with my uncle Slava.",
    "As these and endless other stories about the late 1980s suggest, the system’s collapse had been profoundly unexpected and unimaginable to many Soviet people until it happened, and yet, it quickly appeared perfectly logical and exciting when it began. Many discovered that, unbeknownst to themselves, they had always been ready for it, that they had always known that life in socialism was shaped through a curious paradox, that the system was always felt to be both stagnating and immutable, fragile and vigorous, bleak and full of promise. These experiences suggest an important set of questions about Soviet socialism: What was the nature of the late Soviet system and way of life that had this paradox at its core? On what kind of internal systemic shifts at the level of discourse, ideology, social relations, and time was this paradox predicated? Furthermore, what was the nature of the production and communication of knowledge in this system, and of the forms in which it was coded, circulated, received, and interpreted? These questions are not about the causes for the collapse but about the conditions that made the collapse possible without making it anticipated. With these questions in mind, this book sets out to explore late socialism—the period that spanned approximately thirty years, between the mid-1950s and the mid-1980s, before the changes of perestroika began, when the system was still being experienced as eternal. This book will investigate this period through the eyes of its last generation, focusing on these people’s relations with ideology, discourse, and ritual, and on the multiple unanticipated meanings, communities, relations, identities, interests, and pursuits that these relations allowed to emerge."
  ],

soznania）和“强烈震撼”（sil'neishii shok），紧接着便是兴奋和参与变革的热切意愿。虽然不同的人以不同的方式经历那个时刻，但他们所描述的经验类型是相似的，而且许多人对它记忆犹新。", "托尼娅（Tonya）生于1966年的列宁格勒，是一位学校教师。她描述了自己大约在1987年第一次意识到“某种不可能之事”（chto-to udivleniia），那也发生在大约1987到1988年：“对我来说，改革始于《星火》（Ogonek）5首次刊登[尼古拉]古米廖夫（Gumilev）的几首诗。”古米廖夫是阿克梅派诗人圈子的成员，自1920年代以来，他的诗歌从未在苏联出版过。6伊娜此前已在手抄本中读过这些诗，但从未料到它们会出现在官方出版物上。令她惊讶的不是诗歌本身，而是它们出现在报刊上。", "新出版物的洪流开始呈指数级增长，阅读一切、与朋友交换文本、讨论所读内容的做法，很快成为一种全国性的痴迷。1987年至1988年间，大多数报纸和文学杂志的发行量飙升得惊人，在一年之内增长了十倍甚至更多。7由于售罄速度太快，人们常常无法在报刊亭买到许多更受欢迎的出版物。在写给周刊《星火》的信中，读者抱怨说，为了有机会买到杂志，他们不得不在凌晨5点、也就是报亭开门前两个小时，就在当地的报亭前排起长队。和所有人一样，托尼娅也尽量多读：“我和我的朋友卡佳（Katia）开始订阅月刊文学杂志（tolstye zhurnaly）：《十月》（Oktiabr'）、《我们的同时代人》（Nash Sovremennik）、《新世界》（Novyi Mir）、《旗帜》（Znamia）、《青春》（Iunost'）。大家都尽量订阅不同的杂志，这样就能与朋友交换，接触到更多材料。我们周围的人都在这样做。我花了整整一年时间不停地读这些刊物。”", "阅读杂志、观看电视直播、与同样在做这些事的朋友交谈，很快就催生出新的语言、话题、比较、隐喻和观念，最终导致话语与意识的深刻转变。这一过程的结果是，在1980年代末，人们普遍意识到，那个看似如此永恒的国家社会主义，或许真的正在走向终结。意大利文学学者维托里奥·斯特拉达（Vitorio Strada）在变革开始前曾长期在苏联生活，他概括了自己在1980年代末苏联人民身上所看到的这种快进历史经验：“[没]有人，或者说几乎没有人，能够想象崩溃……竟会来得这么快、这么急。……终结的时机及其发生的方式简直令人震惊”（Strada 1998, 13）。", marshrut）8，然后是索尔仁尼琴，再然后是瓦西里·格罗斯曼（Vasilii Grossman）。9格罗斯曼是第一个暗示共产主义可能是法西斯主义的一种形式的人。这一点我以前从未想到过。他没有公开这么说，而只是比较了两个体制下的酷刑。我记得自己躺在房间的沙发上看这本书，强烈地感到一场革命正在我身边发生。这令人震惊。我的意识发生了断裂（perelom soznania）。接着是弗拉基米尔·沃伊诺维奇（Vladimir Voinovich）的书。我把一切都与我的叔叔斯拉瓦（Slava）分享。", "正如这些以及无数其他关于1980年代末的故事所表明的，体制的崩溃对许多苏联人而言，在发生之前曾是深刻出乎意料、不可想象的；然而，当它开始时，却迅速显得完全合乎逻辑、令人兴奋。许多人发现，他们自己浑然不觉地早已为它做好了准备：他们一直知道，社会主义中的生活是由一个奇特的悖论塑造的，体制始终被感受为既停滞又不可改变、既脆弱又充满活力、既黯淡又充满希望。这些经验提出了一组关于苏联社会主义的重要问题：以这一悖论为核心的晚期苏联体制与生活方式，其本质是什么？这一悖论建立于话语、意识形态、社会关系与时间层面上的何种内在体制转变之上？此外，在这一体制中，知识的生产与传播，以及知识被编码、流通、接收与阐释的形式，其本质又是什么？这些问题关心的不是崩溃的原因，而是那些使崩溃成为可能、却又不使其被预见的条件。带着这些问题，本书着手探索晚期社会主义——这个大约从1950年代中期延续到1980年代中期、跨度约三十年、在改革的种种变化开始之前、体制仍被感受为永恒的时期。本书将通过其最后一代人的眼睛来考察这一时期，聚焦于这些人与意识形态、话语和仪式的关系，以及这些关系所允许浮现出的种种意想不到的意义、社群、关系、身份、兴趣与追求。"]}

"As these and endless other stories about the late 1980s suggest, the system's collapse had been profoundly unexpected and unimaginable to many Soviet people until it happened, and yet, it quickly appeared perfectly logical and exciting when it began. "“我甚至从未想到过，苏联有什么东西会发生变化。更不用说它会消失了。没有人预料到这一点。无论是孩子，还是大人。给人的完整体会是，一切都是永恒的。”著名词曲作者、音乐家安德烈·马卡列维奇（Andrei Makarevich）2 在1994年的一次电视采访中如是说。在后来出版的回忆录中，马卡列维奇回忆道，他像数百万苏联公民一样，一直觉得自己生活在一个永恒的国家（vechnoe gosudarstvo）之中（2002, 14）。直到大约1986年和1987年，当改革（perestroika，重建）已经如火如荼之际，“社会主义制度不会永远延续”的可能性才进入他的脑海。许多其他人也描述了类似的体验：对苏联体制的持久与不变所怀有的深切感受，以及对其崩溃的完全始料未及。然而，马卡列维奇和许多苏联人也很快发现了另一个奇特的事实：尽管崩溃看似突然，他们却发现自己已经为它做好了准备。那些年里，一个奇特的悖论变得明显：尽管体制的崩溃在开始之前是不可想象的，但当它发生时，却显得并不令人意外。"

6. "1985年，当改革（perestroika）与公开性（glasnost'，开放与公开讨论）政策出台时，大多数人并未预料到随后会有任何激进的变化。人们认为，这些运动与此前由国家组织的无穷无尽的运动并无不同：那些运动来了又去，而生活一如既往。然而，一两年之内，某种不可想象的事情正在发生这一认识，开始在苏联人民心中浮现。许多人谈到自己经历了一种突然的“意识断裂”（perelom soznania）和“强烈震撼”（sil'neishii shok），紧接着便是兴奋和参与变革的热切意愿。虽然不同的人以不同的方式经历那个时刻，但他们所描述的经验类型是相似的，而且许多人对它记忆犹新。"

7. "托尼娅（Tonya）生于1966年的列宁格勒，是一位学校教师。她描述了自己大约在1987年第一次意识到“某种不可能之事”（chto-to nevozmozhnoe）正在发生的时刻：“我当时在地铁上读书，突然感到一阵彻底的震惊。那个时刻我记得非常清楚……我正在读列夫"

"拉兹贡（Razgon）的故事《并非虚构》（Nepridumannoe）3，刚刚发表在《青春》杂志（Iunost'）上。我从未想象过，任何哪怕稍有一点点类似的东西会被发表。在那之后，出版物便如洪流般汹涌而来。”伊娜（Inna，1958年生于列宁格勒）4记得她自己“第一个惊讶的时刻”（pervyi moment udivleniia），那也发生在大约1987到1988年：“对我来说，改革始于《星火》（Ogonek）5首次刊登[尼古拉]古米廖夫（Gumilev）的几首诗。”古米廖夫是阿克梅派诗人圈子的成员，自1920年代以来，他的诗歌从未在苏联出版过。6伊娜此前已在手抄本中读过这些诗，但从未料到它们会出现在官方出版物上。令她惊讶的不是诗歌本身，而是它们出现在报刊上。"

"新出版物的洪流开始成倍地高涨，阅读一切、与朋友交换文本、讨论所读内容，这种习惯很快成为一种全国性的痴迷。1987年至1988年间，大多数报纸和文学杂志的发行量飙升得惊人，在一年之内增长了十倍甚至更多。7由于售罄速度太快，人们常常无法在报刊亭买到许多更受欢迎的出版物。在写给周刊《星火》的信中，读者抱怨说，为了有机会买到杂志，他们不得不在凌晨5点、也就是报亭开门前两个小时，就在当地的报亭前排起长队。和所有人一样，托尼娅也尽量多读：“我和我的朋友卡佳（Katia）开始订阅月刊文学杂志（tolstye zhurnaly）：《十月》（Oktiabr'）、《我们的同时代人》（Nash Sovremennik）、《新世界》（Novyi Mir）、《旗帜》（Znamia）、《青春》（Iunost'）。大家都尽量订阅不同的杂志，这样就能与朋友交换，接触到更多材料。我们周围的人都在这样做。我花了整整一年时间不停地读这些刊物。”"

10. "阅读杂志、观看电视直播、与同样在做这些事的朋友交谈，很快就催生出新的语言、话题、比较、隐喻和观念，最终导致话语与意识的深刻转变。这一过程的结果是，在1980年代末，人们普遍意识到，那个看似如此永恒的国有社会主义，或许真的正在走向终结。意大利文学学者维托里奥·斯特拉达（Vitorio Strada）在变革开始前曾长期在苏联生活，他概括了自己在1980年代末苏联人民身上所看到的这种快进历史经验：“[没]有人，或者说几乎没有人，能够想象崩溃……竟会来得这么快、这么急。……终结的时机及其发生的方式简直令人震惊”（Strada 1998, 13）。"

"正如这些以及无数其他关于1980年代末的故事所表明的，体制的崩溃对许多苏联人而言，在发生之前曾是深刻出乎意料、不可想象的；然而，当它开始时，却迅速显得完全合乎逻辑、令人兴奋。许多人发现，他们自己浑然不觉地早已为它做好了准备：他们一直知道，社会主义中的生活是由一个奇特的悖论塑造的，体制始终被感受为既停滞又不可改变、既脆弱又充满活力、既黯淡又充满希望。这些经验提出了一组关于苏联社会主义的重要问题：以这一悖论为核心的晚期苏联体制与生活方式，其本质是什么？这一悖论建立在话语、意识形态、社会关系和时间层面上的何种内在体制转变之上？此外，在这一体制中，知识的生产与传播，以及知识被编码、流通、接收和阐释的形式，其本质又是什么？这些问题关心的不是崩溃的原因，而是那些使崩溃成为可能、却又不使其被预见的条件。带着这些问题，本书着手探索晚期社会主义——这个大约跨越三十年、从1950年代中期到1980年代中期、在改革的种种变化开始之前、体制仍被感受为永恒的时期。本书将通过其最后一代人的眼睛来考察这一时期，聚焦于这些人与意识形态、话语和仪式的关系，以及这些关系所允许浮现出的种种意想不到的意义、社群、关系、身份、兴趣与追求。"

6. "1985年，当改革（perestroika）与公开性（glasnost'，开放与公开讨论）政策出台时，大多数人并未预料到随后会有任何激进的变化。人们认为，这些运动与此前由国家组织的无穷无尽的运动并无不同：那些运动来了又去，而生活一如既往。然而，一两年之内，某种不可想象的事情正在发生这一认识，开始在苏联人民心中浮现。许多人谈到自己经历了一种突然的“意识断裂”（perelom soznania）和“强烈震撼”（sil'neishii shok），紧接着便是兴奋和参与变革的热切意愿。虽然不同的人以不同的方式经历那个时刻，但他们所描述的经验类型是相似的，而且许多人对它记忆犹新。"

"拉兹贡（Razgon）的故事《并非虚构》（Nepridumannoe）3，刚刚发表在《青春》杂志（Iunost'）上。我从未想象过，任何哪怕有一点点类似的东西会被发表。在那之后，出版物便如洪流般汹涌而来。”伊娜（Inna，1958年生于列宁格勒）4记得她自己“第一个惊讶的时刻”（pervyi moment udivleniia），那也发生在大约1987到1988年：“对我来说，改革始于《星火》（Ogonek）5首次刊登[尼古拉]古米廖夫（Gumilev）的几首诗。”古米廖夫是阿克梅派诗人圈子的成员，自1920年代以来，他的诗歌从未在苏联出版过。6伊娜此前已在手抄本中读过这些诗，但从未料到它们会出现在官方出版物上。令她惊讶的不是诗歌本身，而是它们出现在报刊上。"

翻译时结合并遵守其他输入字段提供的信息。

{
  "sources": [
    "## Binary Socialism",
    "One of the motivations for writing this book is to question certain problematic assumptions about Soviet socialism, which are implicitly and explicitly reproduced in much academic and journalistic writing today. These common assumptions include the following: socialism was “bad” and “immoral” or had been experienced as such by Soviet people before the changes of perestroika, and, further, the collapse of Soviet socialism was predicated on this badness and immorality. These assumptions are manifest today in the terminology used to describe that system—for example, in the widespread use of phrases such as “the Soviet regime,” with the myriad assumptions often packed into it—and in the use of binary categories to describe Soviet reality such as oppression and resistance, repression and freedom, the state and the people, official economy and second economy, oficial culture and counterculture, totalitarian language and counterlanguage, public self and private self, truth and lie, reality and dissimulation, morality and corruption, and so on.10 These terminologies have occupied a dominant position in the accounts of Soviet socialism produced in the West and, since the end of socialism, in the former Soviet Union as well.",
    "In the most extreme examples of this discourse, Soviet citizens are portrayed as having no agency: in this portrayal, they allegedly subscribed to “communist values” either because they were coerced to do so or because they had no means of reflecting upon them critically. In the late 1980s, Françoise Thom argued that, in the context of ubiquitous ideological language, linguistic “symbols cease[d] to work properly,” making the Soviet Union “a world without meaning, without events and without humanity” (Thom 1989, 156). In the late 1990s, Frank Ellis went further:",
    "“When reason, common sense, and decency are assaulted often enough, then personality is crippled, and human intelligence disintegrates or is warped. The barrier between truth and lies is effectively destroyed. . . . Schooled in such a climate, fearful and deprived of any intellectual initiative, Homo Sovieticus could never be more than a mouthpiece for the party’s ideas and slogans, not so much a human being then, as a receptacle to be emptied and filled as party policy dictated.” (Ellis 1998, 208)",
    "Even when granted some agency in accounts of this type, the voices of these subjects are often still unheard due to oppression and fear. For example, John Young describes Soviet citizens as “non-conforming” dissidents, who “counter the deceptions of government by seting forth ‘the facts’ in contrast to oficial falsehood” in “conversations with frustrated friends behind closed doors, in sign language devised by family members who suspect the secret police have bugged their apartment, in a manuscript or on a tape recording passed around from person to person” (Young 1991, 226). These are extreme examples; however, they represent a definite trend in conceptualizing Soviet life.11",
    "Binary metaphors are also widespread in retrospective analyses of socialism writen inside the former Soviet Union since the “collapse.” In such accounts, Soviet culture is divided into the “oficial” and the “unoficial”—a division that, according to sociologists Uvarova and Rogov, can be traced back to a particular dissident ideology of the 1970s which held that “nothing good could appear in an [oficial] Soviet journal in principle; and a real text could only be published in an unoficial publication (samizdat) or a foreign publication (tamizdat)” (1998). Critiquing this division, Uvarova and Rogov propose instead to divide Soviet culture into censored (podtsenzurnaia) and uncensored (nepodtsenzurnaia). This change of terms helps to highlight the ambivalence of cultural production in the Soviet Union; however, it still reduces Soviet reality to a binary division between the state (censored) and the society beyond it (uncensored), failing to account for the fact that many of the common cultural phenomena in socialism that were allowed, tolerated, or even promoted within the realm of the oficially censored were nevertheless quite distinct from the ideological texts of the Party.",
    "One reason for the persistence of these binary models is the particular “situatedness” (Haraway 1991) of much critical knowledge about Soviet socialism: it has been produced either outside of, or in retrospect to, socialism, in contexts dominated by antisocialist, nonsocialist, or post-socialist political, moral, and cultural agendas and truths. As Rogov demonstrates in his research, diaries from Brezhnev’s period, produced during the 1970s, and memoirs produced retrospectively in the 1990s are not only writen in two distinct voices and languages; they also evaluate the everyday realities of Soviet socialism, both implicitly and explicitly, in two dif­ erent ways. The memoirs not only tend to be much more critical of the socialist system than the diaries, but also to conceive of it and of the author’s place within it in terms that emerged only in retrospect (Rogov 1998).12 Patrick Seriot has also shown that by the end of perestroika in the late 1980s, it had become politically important, especially for members of the intelligentsia, to emphasize that during socialism there was no “mixing [of] the language of power with their own language” and that their own language was “a free space to be extended through struggle” (Seriot 1992, 205–6). But this story of divided languages was, to a large extent, a retrospective late- and post-perestroika construction.",
    "Furthermore, the term stagnation (zastoi), which figures prominently as a tag for the period of Brezhnev’s rule, also emerged only in retrospect, during the time of Gorbachev’s reforms, after Brezhnev’s period had ended and the socialist system was undergoing its rapid transformation.13 In fact, the very conceptualization of the late 1960s and 1970s, when Brezhnev was the party’s general secretary, as a certain “period” with concrete historical features, also emerged retrospectively during perestroika. According to Rogov, “The [Soviet] person in the 1970s had a rather vague understanding about the historical coordinates of his epoch, considerably vaguer than became apparent to the same person from the perspective of the late 1980s and 1990s” (1998, 7). The perestroika critical discourse which exposed many unknown facts about the Soviet past and critically articulated many realities that had been implicitly known but unarticulated until then, also contributed to the creation of certain myths about it that were colored by the newly emergent revolutionary ideas and political agendas of the late 1980s. Many binary categories in the accounts of the vanishing system gained their prominence within that revolutionary context.",
    "At the same time, some of the roots of these binary categories go much deeper, originating in the broad “regimes of knowledge” formed under the conditions of the Cold War, when the entity of “the Soviet bloc” had been articulated in opposition to “the West” and as distinct from “the third world.” The act of critiquing isolated binaries does not necessarily deconstruct these deeper underlying assumptions behind them. For example, Susan Gal and Gail Kligman provided a crucial critique of many binary divisions that dominate the studies of state socialism, arguing that in these societies “[r]ather than any clear-cut ‘us’ versus ‘them’ or ‘private’ versus ‘public,’ there was a ubiquitous self-embedding or interweaving of these categories.”14 And yet, they connected this critique with another claim that “[e]veryone was to some extent complicit in the system of patronage, lying, theft, hedging, and duplicity through which the system operated,” and that often even “intimates, family members and friends informed on each other” (Gal and Kligman 2000, 51). The emphasis on such categories as duplicity, lying, and informing on others—which suggest moral quandaries at the core of the people’s relations with the system and with each other— implicitly reproduces an underlying assumption that socialism was based on a complex web of immoralities."

function.arguments: {"targets": ["## 二元社会主义", "本书的写作动机之一，是要质疑关于苏联社会主义的某些成问题的假设——这些假设今天在许多学术与新闻写作中被或隐或显地再生产出来。这些常见的假设包括：社会主义是\"坏的\"\"不道德的\"，或苏联人民在改革（perestroika）带来的变化之前正是如此体验它的；此外，苏联社会主义的崩溃正是以这种坏与不道德为前提的。今天，这些假设既显见于描述该制度的术语之中——例如广泛使用的\"苏联政权\"（the Soviet regime）这类短语，其中往往承载着无数假设——也显见于用来描述苏联现实的种种二元范畴之中，如压迫与抵抗、压制与自由、国家与人民、官方经济与第二经济、官方文化与反文化、极权语言与反语言、公开的自我与私下的自我、真理与谎言、现实与伪装、道德与腐败，等等。10 这些术语在西方关于苏联社会主义的叙述中占据着主导地位，而且自社会主义终结以来，在前苏联地区也同样如此。", "在这一话语最极端的例子里，苏联公民被描绘成毫无能动性：按照这种描绘，他们之所以认同\"共产主义价值\"，要么是出于被迫，要么是因为他们没有任何手段对其进行批判性反思。1980年代末，弗朗索瓦丝·托姆（Françoise Thom）提出，在无处不在的意识形态语言语境中，语言的\"象征[开始]失去正常功能\"，使苏联成为\"一个没有意义、没有事件、也没有人性的世界\"（Thom 1989, 156）。1990年代末，弗兰克·埃利斯（Frank Ellis）走得更远：", "\"当理性、常识与体面受到足够频繁的侵犯时，人格便被摧残，人的智识要么分崩离析，要么扭曲变形。真理与谎言之间的界线被有效地摧毁了……在这样的气候中受训，心怀恐惧、又丧失了一切智识主动性的苏维埃人（Homo Source 3:
"在这一话语最极端的例子里，苏联公民被描绘成毫无能动性：按照这种描绘，他们之所以认同"共产主义价值"，要么是出于被迫，要么是因为他们没有任何手段对其进行批判性反思。1980年代末，弗朗索瓦丝·托姆（Françoise Thom）提出，在无处不在的意识形态语言语境中，语言的"象征[开始]失去正常功能"，使苏联成为"一个没有意义、没有事件、也没有人性的世界"（Thom 1989, 156）。1990年代末，弗兰克·埃利斯（Frank Ellis）走得更远："

""当理性、常识与体面受到足够频繁的侵犯时，人格便被摧残，人的智识要么分崩离析，要么扭曲变形。真理与谎言之间的界线被有效地摧毁了……在这样的气候中受训，心怀恐惧、又丧失了一切智识主动性的苏维埃人（Homo Sovieticus）永远只能是党的思想与口号的传声筒——与其说是一个活生生的人，不如说是一个容器，随党的政策的指示被倒空、被填满。"（Ellis 1998, 208）"

Source 4:
"即便在这类叙述中承认这些主体拥有一定的能动性，由于压迫与恐惧，他们的声音往往依然不为人所闻。例如，约翰·扬（John Young）把苏联公民描述为"不驯从"的持不同政见者，他们在"关起门来与沮丧的朋友的谈话中、在怀疑秘密警察已窃听公寓的家庭成员设计的手势语中、在从一个人手中传到另一个人手中的手稿或录音带上"，"摆出'事实'以对抗官方的谎言"（Young 1991, 226）。这些是极端的例子；然而，它们代表着将苏联生活概念化的一种明确趋势。11"

Source 5:
"二元隐喻在"崩溃"以来前苏联境内对社会主义的回顾性分析中同样普遍。在这类叙述中，苏联文化被划分为"官方的"与"非官方的"——据社会学家乌瓦罗娃（Uvarova）与罗戈夫（Rogov）的说法，这种划分可以追溯到1970年代一种特定的持不同政见者意识形态，即认为"好的东西原则上不可能出现在[官方的]苏联期刊上；真正的文本只能发表在非官方出版物（地下出版物，samizdat）或外国出版物（境外出版物，tamizdat）中"（1998）。在批评这种划分时，乌瓦罗娃与罗戈夫提议改而将苏联文化划分为受审查的（podtsenzurnaia）与不受审查的（nepodtsenzurnaia）。这种术语的更改有助于凸显苏联文化生产的矛盾性；然而，它仍将苏联现实简化为国家（受审查）与其之外的社会（不受审查）之间的二元划分，未能说明这样一个事实：在官方审查的领域内被允许、被容忍甚至被推动的许多常见的社会主义文化现象，却与党的意识形态文本颇为不同。"

Source 6:
"这些二元模式之所以持续存在，一个原因在于，关于苏联社会主义的许多批判性知识具有特定的"情境性"（situatedness，哈拉维1991）：这些知识要么产生于社会主义之外，要么是回顾性地产生的，其语境由反社会主义、非社会主义或后社会主义的政治、道德与文化议程及"真理"所主导。正如罗戈夫在其研究中所表明的，勃列日涅夫时期的日记（写于1970年代）与1990年代回顾性写成的回忆录，不仅以两种不同的声音与语言写成；它们对苏联社会主义日常现实的评价，无论隐性地还是显性地，也以两种不同的方式进行。回忆录不仅往往比日记对社会主义制度的批评尖锐得多，而且是以只有在回顾中才出现的术语来构想该制度以及作者在其中的位置的（Rogov 1998）。12 帕特里克·塞里奥（Patrick Seriot）也表明，到1980年代末改革接近尾声之际，强调在社会主义时期不存在"权力语言与自身语言的混用"、自己的语言是"有待通过斗争加以拓展的自由空间"（Seriot 1992, 205–6），在政治上已变得尤为重要，尤其是对知识分子而言。但这段语言分裂的故事，在很大程度上是改革末期与后改革时期的一种回顾性建构。"

function.arguments: {"targets": ["## 日常现实", "苏联体制造成了巨大的苦难、压迫、恐惧与自由的匮乏，凡此种种皆有翔实记载。但如果我们想要回答本书所提出的、关于社会主义生活内在悖论的问题，仅仅关注该体制的这一面并不能让我们走得很远。在二元叙述中往往被忽略的，是这样一种至关重要且看似悖论的事实：对大量苏联公民而言，社会主义生活的许多基本价值、理想与现实（如平等、社群、无私、利他、友谊、伦理关系、安全、教育、劳动、创造以及对未来的关切）具有真正的重要性，尽管他们的许多日常实践惯常地逾越、重新阐释或拒绝了社会主义国家官方意识形态所呈现的某些规范与规则。对许多人来说，作为一套人类价值体系、并作为\"正常生活\"（normal'naia zhizn'）15之日常现实的\"社会主义\"，未必等同于\"国家\"或\"意识形态\"；事实上，对他们而言，亲历社会主义往往意味着与官方言辞所提供的阐释相当不同的事物。", "当今\"后苏联怀旧\"现象——一种复杂的后苏联建构16——有一个不可否认的构成性成分，即对社会主义现实所提供的、非常真实的人道价值、伦理、友谊与创造可能性的怀念；这些价值与可能性往往是顶着国家的宣告目标而存在的，它们与沉闷感和疏离感一样，都是社会主义日常生活不可化约的组成部分。一位俄罗斯哲学家1995年写道，从苏联解体最初几年的视角来看，他已逐渐认识到，苏联现实的灰暗与恐惧，同一种非常真实的乐观与温情——连同在\"陈设良好的共同生活空间\"里的种种\"人的幸福\"、\"舒适与安康\"和\"热忱、成功与秩序\"——密不可分地联系在一起（Savchuk 1995）。一位俄罗斯摄影师呼应着同样的领悟，作了一番\"平庸的自白\"：对他个人而言，回顾之下，\"共产主义的崩溃\"同时也是某种非常个人化、纯真而充满希望之物的崩溃，是那种标志着童年与青年的\"热烈的真诚与率真\"的崩溃（Vilenskii 1995）。对这类回顾进行批判性的审视，对于理解苏联社会主义不可或缺。如果不理解\"现实存在的社会主义\"在众多公民生活中所获得的伦理与审美悖论，如果不理解他们赋予自己社会主义生活的那种创造性、积极的意义——这些意义有时与国家的宣告目标一致，有时与之相悖，有时又以种种并不契合非此即彼二元对立的方式与之相关——我们就无法理解社会主义究竟是怎样一种社会制度，也无法理解为何它的突然转变对生活在其中的人们而言如此难以想象，却又并不令人意外。", "要分析否定价值与肯定价值、疏离与依恋这种看似悖论的混杂，我们需要一种语言：它不把对社会主义现实的描述化约为官方与非官方、国家与人民的二元对立，也不化约为在冷战意识形态中形成的道德判断。后殖民研究中近来关于语言的批判性讨论，为社会主义语境提供了某些相关洞见。17 迪佩什·查卡拉巴提批评某些后殖民史学使用一种语言，这种语言含蓄地把\"欧洲\"生产为\"一切历史——包括我们称之为'印度'、'中国'、'肯尼亚'等等的历史——的主权性理论主体\"，把其他这些历史化约为\"可被称为'欧洲史'的主导叙事的种种变体\"（2000, 27）。查卡拉巴提呼吁一种能够消解中心、\"地方化\"后殖民史学中欧洲\"主导叙事\"的语言，这一呼吁同样适用于关于社会主义的著述；然而，就社会主义而言，尤其是在俄国，\"地方化\"的对象将不仅仅是\"欧洲\"，而更具体地是\"西欧\"18——即社会主义史中一种后苏联的\"主导叙事\"，它含蓄而明确地再生产着冷战的二元范畴以及\"第一世界\"与\"第二世界\"之间的对立。", "本书也是对这种语言的一次寻找，并借此重构社会主义生活的某些伦理与审美复杂性，以及它所呈现的那些创造性、富于想象、往往又充满悖论的文化形式。这一任务面临的挑战，是在避免对社会主义作先验的否定性叙述的同时，又不落入将其浪漫化的相反极端。通过展现现实存在的社会主义的真实情形——在那里，控制、强制、疏离、恐惧与道德困境，同理想、社群伦理、尊严、创造和对未来的关怀不可化约地交织在一起——本书试图观照并重新赋予苏联社会主义生活以人性。19"]}

"The Soviet system produced tremendous sufering, repression, fear, and lack of freedom, all of which are well documented. But focusing only on that side of the system will not take us very far if we want to answer the question posed by this book about the internal paradoxes of life under socialism. What tends to get lost in the binary accounts is the crucial and seemingly paradoxical fact that, for great numbers of Soviet citizens, many of the fundamental values, ideals, and realities of socialist life (such as equality, community, selflessness, altruism, friendship, ethical relations, safety, education, work, creativity, and concern for the future) were of genuine importance, despite the fact that many of their everyday practices routinely transgressed, reinterpreted, or refused certain norms and rules represented in the oficial ideology of the socialist state. For many, "socialism" as a system of human values and as an everyday reality of "normal life" (normal'naia zhizn')15 was not necessarily equivalent to "the state" or "ideology"; indeed, living socialism to them often meant something quite different from the oficial interpretations provided by state rhetoric."

Translation:
"苏联体制造成了巨大的苦难、压迫、恐惧与自由的匮乏，凡此种种皆有翔实记载。但如果我们想回答本书所提出的、关于社会主义生活内在悖论的问题，仅仅关注该体制的这一面并不能使我们走得很远。在二元论叙述中往往被忽略的是一个至关重要且看似悖论的事实：对大量苏联公民而言，社会主义生活的许多基本价值、理想与现实（如平等、社群、无私、利他、友谊、伦理关系、安全、教育、劳动、创造以及对未来的关切）具有真正的重要性，尽管他们的许多日常实践惯常地逾越、重新阐释或拒绝了社会主义国家官方意识形态所代表的某些规范与规则。对许多人来说，作为一套人类价值体系、同时作为"正常生活"（normal'naia zhizn'）15之日常现实的"社会主义"，未必等同于"国家"或"意识形态"；事实上，对他们而言，过社会主义的生活往往意味着与官方言辞所提供的阐释相当不同的事物。"

Source 3:
"An undeniable constitutive part of today's phenomenon of "post-Soviet nostalgia," which is a complex post-Soviet construct,16 is the longing for the very real humane values, ethics, friendships, and creative possibilities that the reality of socialism aforded—often in spite of the state's proclaimed goals—and that were as irreducibly part of the everyday life of socialism as were the feelings of dullness and alienation. A Russian philosopher wrote in 1995 that, from the vantage point of the first post-Soviet years, he had come to recognize that the grayness and fear of Soviet reality had been indivisibly linked with a very real optimism and warmth, with accompanying forms of "human happiness," "comforts and well-being," and "cordiality, successes and order" in a "well-furnished common space of living" (Savchuk 1995). A Russian photographer, echoing the same realization, made a "banal confession" that for him personally the "crash of Communism" was also, in retrospect, the crash of something very personal, innocent, and full of hope, of the "passionate sincerity and genuineness" that marked childhood and youth (Vilenskii 1995). A critical examination of such retrospections is essential to an understanding of Soviet socialism. Without understanding the ethical and aesthetic paradoxes that "really existing socialism" acquired in the lives of many of its citizens, and without understanding the creative and positive meanings with which they endowed their socialist lives— sometimes in line with the announced goals of the state, sometimes in spite of them, and sometimes relating to them in ways that did not fit either-or dichotomies—we would fail to understand what kind of social system socialism was and why its sudden transformation was so unimaginable and yet unsurprising to the people living within it."

Translation:
"当今"后苏联怀旧"现象（一种复杂的后苏联建构）16中一个不可否认的构成性成分，是对社会主义现实所提供的那些非常真实的人道价值、伦理、友谊与创造可能性的怀念——这些往往与国家的宣告目标背道而驰——而它们与沉闷感和疏离感一样，都不可化约地属于社会主义日常生活的一部分。一位俄罗斯哲学家在1995年写道，从苏联解体最初几年的视角回望，他开始认识到，苏联现实的灰暗与恐惧同一种非常真实的乐观与温情密不可分地联系在一起，伴随着在"陈设良好的共同生活空间"（Savchuk 1995）中的种种"人的幸福"、"舒适与安康"以及"热忱、成功与秩序"的形式。一位俄罗斯摄影师呼应同样的领悟，作了一番"平庸的忏悔"：对他来说，回顾之下，"共产主义的崩溃"同时也是某种非常个人、纯真而充满希望之物的崩溃，是标志着童年与青年的"热烈的真诚与率真"的崩溃（Vilenskii 1995）。对这类回顾进行批判性的审视，对于理解苏联社会主义不可或缺。若不理解"现实存在的社会主义"在众多公民生活中所获得的伦理与审美悖论，若不理解他们赋予自己社会主义生活的那些创造性、积极的意义——有时与国家的宣告目标一致，有时与之相悖，有时又以种种并不契合非此即彼二元对立的方式与之相关——我们便无法理解社会主义究竟是怎样一种社会制度，也无法理解为何它的突然转变对生活在其中的人们而言既如此难以想象，却又并不令人意外。"

Source 4:
"For the analysis of this seemingly paradoxical mix of the negative and positive values, of alienations and atachments, we need a language that does not reduce the description of socialist reality to dichotomies of the oficial and the unoficial, the state and the people, and to moral judgments shaped within cold war ideologies. Recent critical discussion of language from postcolonial studies provides some insight relevant to the socialist context.17 Dipesh Chakrabarty criticizes some postcolonial historiography for the use of a kind of language that implicitly produces "Europe" as "the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call 'Indian,' 'Chinese,' 'Kenyan,' and so on," reducing these other histories to "variations on a master narrative that could be called 'the history of Europe'" (2000, 27). Chakrabarty's call for a language that would decenter and "provincialize" the "master narrative" of Europe in postcolonial historiography is relevant to the writings on socialism; however, in the case of socialism, especially in Russia, the object of "provincializing" would not just be "Europe" but, more specifically, "Western Europe"18—a post-Soviet "master narrative" in the history of socialism that implicitly and explicitly reproduces binary categories of the Cold War and of the opposition between "first world" and "second world.""

Translation:
"要分析这种否定价值与肯定价值、疏离与依恋看似悖论性的混杂，我们需要一种语言，它不把对社会主义现实的描述化约为官方与非官方、国家与人民的二元对立，也不化约为在冷战意识形态中形成的道德判断。后殖民研究中近期关于语言的批判性讨论，为社会主义语境提供了某些相关洞见。17 迪佩什·查卡拉巴提批评某些后殖民史学使用一种语言，这种语言含蓄地把"欧洲"制造为"一切历史——包括我们称为'印度'、'中国'、'肯尼亚'等等的历史——的主权性理论主体"，把这些其他历史化约为"可称为'欧洲史'的主导叙事的种种变体"（2000, 27）。查卡拉巴提呼吁一种能够消解中心、把后殖民史学中的"主导叙事"加以"地方化"的语言，这一呼吁与关于社会主义的著述相关；然而，就社会主义而言，尤其是在俄国，"地方化"的对象将不只是"欧洲"，而更具体地是"西欧"18——即社会主义史中一种后苏联的"主导叙事"，它含蓄而明确地再生产着冷战以及"第一世界"与"第二世界"对立的二元范畴。"

Source 5:
"This book is also an atempt to look for such a language and thereby to reconstruct some ethical and aesthetic complexities of socialist life, as well as the creative, imaginative, and often paradoxical cultural forms that it took. The challenge of such a task is to avoid a priori negative accounts of socialism without falling into the opposite extreme of romanticizing it. By showing the realities of actually existing socialism—where control, coercion, alienation, fear, and moral quandaries were irreducibly mixed with ideals, communal ethics, dignity, creativity, and care for the future—this book atempts to contemplate and rehumanize Soviet socialist life.19"

你是翻译 Agent。
用户输入是一个翻译 batch，各字段含义如下：
- sources：本批需要翻译的原文列表；
- glossary_terms：翻译时应遵守的术语及固定译法；
- style：目标译文的风格要求；
- context：当前文本之前的局部上下文；
- book_synopsis：全书主题、背景和主线概览；
- chapter_digest：截至当前 batch 之前已经确认的累计章节梗概。

你的基本任务是翻译 sources 中的全部原文。输出译文是与 sources 等长的列表，按下标对应。
翻译时结合并遵守其他输入字段提供的信息。

{
  "sources": [
    "## Lefort’s Paradox",
    "Like Western democracy, Soviet socialism was part of modernity. Foucault stressed that even such “pathological forms” of power as Stalinism and fascism, “in spite of their historical uniqueness . . . are not quite original. They used and extended mechanisms already present in most other societies . . . [and] used to a large extent the ideas and the devices of our political rationality” (Foucault 1983, 209). As a modern project, Soviet socialism shared the key contradictions of modernity.",
    "One of the central contradictions of socialism is a version of what Claude Lefort called a general paradox within the ideology of modernity: the split between ideological enunciation (which reflects the theoretical ideals of the Enlightenment) and ideological rule (manifest in the practical concerns of the modern state’s political authority). The paradox, that we will call “Lefort’s paradox,” lies in the fact that ideological rule must be “abstracted from any question concerning its origins,” thus remaining outside of ideological enunciation and, as a result, rendering that enunciation deficient. In other words, to fulfill its political function of reproducing power, the ideological discourse must claim to represent an “objective truth” that exists outside of it; however, the external nature of this “objective truth” renders the ideological discourse inherently lacking in the means to describe it in total, which can ultimately undermine this discourse’s legitimacy and the power that it supports. This inherent contradiction of any version of modern ideology, argues Lefort, can be concealed only by the figure of the “master,” who, by being presented as standing outside ideological discourse and possessing external knowledge of the objective truth, temporarily conceals the contradiction by allowing it “to appear through himself ” (1986, 211–12).20 In other words, modern ideological discourse, based on the utopian ideals of the Enlightenment, gains its legitimacy from an imaginary position that is external to it and will experience a crisis of legitimacy if that imaginary external position is questioned or destroyed.",
    "In the society built on communist ideals, this paradox appeared through the announced objective of achieving the full liberation of the society and individual (building of communism, creation of the New Man) by means of subsuming that society and individual under full party control. The Soviet citizen was called upon to submit completely to party leadership, to cultivate a collectivist ethic, and repress individualism, while at the same time becoming an enlightened and independentminded individual who pursues knowledge and is inquisitive and creative.21 This Soviet version of Lefort’s paradox was not a chance development; it grew out of the very revolutionary project itself. In 1825, Saint-Simon, an early theorist of the political, intellectual, and artistic avant-garde, whose ideas influenced Marx, Lenin, and Russian revolutionaries, wrote that the project of liberating the society required establishing a political and aesthetic avant-garde that would exercise “over society a positive power, a true priestly function . . . marching forcefully in the van of all the intellectual faculties.” This avantgarde, wrote Saint-Simon, should address itself “to the imagination and to the sentiments of mankind [and] should therefore always exercise the liveliest and most decisive action.” For this purpose the arts and politics should unite under “a common drive and a general idea” (quoted in Egbert 1967, 343).",
    "The conception of a political and artistic avant-garde as a creative force united by one idea for the purposes of leading and perfecting society put this tandem before an enduring paradox: the process of leading and perfecting had to be subsumed under the control of a political program and, at the same time, to be free from control in order to focus on the creative, experimental, and innovating process for the production of a beter future (Egbert 1967, 343–46).",
    "In the Russian revolutionary context, this paradox of modern ideology became institutionalized by the Bolshevik Revolution of 1917. The new process of cultural production was supposed to advance radical social ideas and revolutionize consciousness by achieving two relatively incommensurable goals: to practice an experimental, innovative aesthetics that was constantly ready to defy old canons and, at the same time, to subsume these creative experimentations and innovations under the strict control of the vanguard party. Immediately after the revolution, Lenin wrote in a letter to Clara Zetkin that Communists could not sit in idleness allowing the “cultural process” to develop chaotically: they “must strive with clear consciousness to control that entire process in order to form and define its results” (Arnol’dov et al. 1984, 176). Lenin accused members of the Second International of separatism because some of them argued that, having come to power, the proletariat should stop interfering with creative cultural production and experimentation. On the contrary, argued Lenin, the only means of achieving the goal of the ultimate liberation of culture and consciousness in communism was to intensify the party’s management of all spheres of cultural life. A person could not become truly liberated spontaneously; that person had to be educated and cultivated. On Lenin’s insistence, the Bolshevik Party adopted a resolution stressing that all organizations of the Proletkul’t (People’s Commissariat of Pro letarian Culture) had “an unconditional obligation to regard themselves as strictly subsidiary organs” to the organizations of the Narkompros (People’s Commissariat of Enlightenment) (Arnol’dov et al. 1984, 171). In other words, cultural organizations (all forms of intellectual, scientific, and artistic practice) were subsidiary to educational and political organizations, and all forms of cultural production were to be fully supervised by the party. It was that subsidiary position, went the argument, that would allow these organizations to exercise their full creative potential for the building of the new society.",
    "The Soviet state’s constant anxiety about publicly justifying state control of cultural production while simultaneously attempting to promote its independence and experimentation reflected this paradox. As late as 1984, a book entitled Marxist-Leninist Theory of Culture (Marksistsko-leninskaia teoriia kul’tury), authored by a collective of theoreticians of culture from Moscow’s Institute of Marxism-Leninism (Arnol’dov et al.), was still defending this point. Some may say—their book begins—that to be truly creative, the work of cultural production in intellectual, scientific, and artistic fields cannot be controlled and directed. The book goes on to argue that although this view is not altogether erroneous, it tells only one side of the story, ignoring the irreducible duality of all cultural production. In fact, the book argues, creative work is always both “a strictly private affair” of a creative individual and a “labor of social utility” that creates “spiritual values” and “socio-moral norms” in society. In the socialist society, both aspects of cultural production are recognized as equally important, since in this society “the formation of the new person goes not spontaneously, but consciously, as a result of a purposeful educational work.” Therefore, in the socialist context, the independence of creativity and the control of creative work by the party are not mutually contradictory but must be pursued simultaneously (Arnol’dov et al. 1984, 162, 163). What is remarkable about the discourse in this book is not the argument itself but that this imaginary dispute needed to be revisited throughout Soviet history, suggesting the enduring tension at socialism’s core.",
    "This tension was not limited to scientific and artistic spheres but concerned all discourses and forms of knowledge that were produced and circulated in Soviet society. In the earlier periods of Soviet history, as the following chapters will show, the loud voices of the political, scientific, and artistic avant-garde concealed this paradox. They located themselves “outside” the field of ideological discourse and from that external position made public comments about and adjustments to that discourse. An explosion of creativity and experimentation marked the early postrevolutionary years but ultimately gave way to the suppression of the intellectual avant-garde and all experimental culture and science and to the introduction of a strict and unified party control.22 This shift was enabled and made to appear logical by the paradox inherent in the very ideology of the revolutionary project.",
    "It was Stalin who now played the role of Lefort’s “master” who stood outside of ideological discourse, making editorial comments about it from that external position and in this way concealing the paradox through himself. This external position enabled the production and wide circulation of a public metadiscourse about all forms of political, artistic, and scientific expression that evaluated them for precision and accuracy against an external canon—the Marxist-Leninist dogma. Stalin’s “external” editorial position vis-à-vis all forms of discourse and knowledge, which provided him with unique access to the external canon against which to evaluate them, was crucial in the emergence of those phenomena that became the trademarks of his regime: his immense political power; the cult of his personality; his personal involvement in editing political speeches, scientific papers, films, and musical compositions; the campaign of purges in party organizations; and the ultimate Great Terror in which millions perished. In the last years of Stalin’s rule, and especially after his death in 1953 and the subsequent denunciation of his cult of personality, that external position vis-à-vis discourse and knowledge vanished. The main result of this development was not the denunciation of a concrete leader, but a major reorganization of the entire discursive regime of state socialism: a position external to ideological (political, scientific, artistic) discourse, from which a metadiscourse about it could be launched, ceased to exist, and therefore the metadiscourse on ideology disappeared from public circulation (see discussion of this process in chapter 2).",
    "Since there was no longer an external voice that could conceal the Lefort’s paradox of Soviet ideology, the incongruence of goals and means that constituted that paradox became unleashed. This change ultimately led to a profound transformation of the structure of all types of Soviet ideological discourse (from the language of ideology to the nature of ideological rituals, practices, and organizations) during late socialism. As a result of that transformation, it became less important to read ideological representations for “literal” (referential) meanings than to reproduce their precise structural forms. This transformation of the discursive regime eventually led to a profound shift within Soviet culture during the late period, opening up spaces of indeterminacy, creativity, and unanticipated meanings in the context of strictly formulaic ideological forms, rituals, and organizations. In this way Lefort’s paradox returned to haunt the Soviet system. It enabled a profound internal reinterpretation and displacement of the socialist system, creating a set of contradictory conditions that made the system’s implosion seem so unexpected when it began, and at the same time so unsurprising and fast once it had occurred."
  ],

function.arguments: {"targets": ["## 列斐伏尔的悖论", "与西方民主一样，苏联社会主义也是现代性的一部分。福柯强调，即便是斯大林主义和法西斯主义这类权力的“病理形式”，“尽管有其历史独特性……也并不怎么原创。它们使用并扩展了大多数其他社会中早已存在的机制……并且在很大程度上沿用了我们政治理性的观念与装置”（Foucault 1983, 209）。作为一个现代性工程，苏联社会主义也承载着现代性的关键矛盾。", "社会主义的核心矛盾之一，是克洛德·列斐伏尔所称现代性意识形态内部一种普遍悖论的变体：即意识形态表述（反映启蒙运动的理论理想）与意识形态统治（体现于现代国家政治权威的实际关切）之间的分裂。我们称之为“列斐伏尔的悖论”的这一悖论在于：意识形态统治必须“抽离于任何与其起源相关的问题”，从而置身于意识形态表述之外，并因此使这种表述有所欠缺。换言之，为履行其再生产权力的政治功能，意识形态话语必须声称自己代表着一种存在于自身之外的“客观真理”；然而，这种“客观真理”的外在性，使意识形态话语在根本上缺乏完整描述它的手段，这最终可能削弱该话语的合法性及其所支撑的权力。列斐伏尔认为，任何版本的现代意识形态所固有的这一矛盾，唯有靠“主人”这一形象才能掩盖：主人被呈现为立于意识形态话语之外、拥有关于客观真理的外在知识，从而让这一矛盾“通过他本人显现出来”（1986, 211–12），暂时将其掩盖。20 换言之，基于启蒙运动乌托邦理想的现代意识形态话语，其合法性来自一个外在于自身的想象性位置；一旦这一想象性的外在位置遭到质疑或被摧毁，它便会遭遇合法性危机。", "在建立在共产主义理想之上的社会里，这一悖论通过一个公开宣示的目标而显现：即借助将社会和个人完全纳入党的控制，来实现社会与个人的彻底解放（建设共产主义、造就新人）。苏联公民被号召完全服从党的领导、培育集体主义伦理、压抑个人主义，同时又要成为开明而独立思考的个人——追求知识、好奇而富有创造力。21 这一苏联版本的列斐伏尔悖论并非偶然的发展；它就生长于革命工程自身之中。1825年，圣西门——政治、知识与艺术先锋派的早期理论家，其思想影响了马克思、列宁和俄国革命者——写道，解放社会的工程要求建立一个政治与美学先锋派，它对“社会行使一种积极的力量、一种真正的祭司职能……强有力地行进在一切理智能力的最前列”。圣西门写道，这一先锋派应当诉诸“人类的想象与情感，[并]因此应当始终发挥最活跃、最果断的作用”。为此，艺术与政治应当在“共同的驱动力和总的观念”之下联合起来（转引自 Egbert 1967, 343）。", "将政治与艺术先锋派设想为以单一观念联合起来、旨在引领和完善社会的创造性力量，这一构想使这一对组合面临一个持久的悖论：引领与完善的过程既必须被纳入某个政治纲领的控制之下，同时又必须摆脱控制，以便专注于创造、实验与创新的过程，从而生产出一个更美好的未来（Egbert 1967, 343–46）。", "在俄国革命语境中，现代意识形态的这一悖论因1917年的布尔什维克革命而得以制度化。新的文化生产进程本应通过实现两个相对不可通约的目标来推进激进的社会观念、革命化人的意识：一方面践行一种实验性、创新性的美学，时刻准备挑战旧有的规范；另一方面，又要将这些创造性的实验与创新置于先锋党的严格控制之下。革命刚刚结束，列宁就在致克拉拉·蔡特金的信中写道，共产党人不能袖手旁观，任由“文化进程”混乱地发展：他们“必须以清醒的意识努力控制整个进程，以便形成并规定其结果”（Arnol'dov et al. 1984, 176）。列宁指责第二国际成员搞分裂主义，因为其中一些人主张，无产阶级一旦掌权，就应当停止干预创造性的文化生产与实验。恰恰相反，列宁论证道，要在共产主义中实现文化与意识的最终解放，唯一途径就是加强党对文化生活一切领域的管理。人不可能自发地获得真正的解放；人必须被教育、被培养。在列宁的坚持下，布尔什维克党通过了一项决议，强调无产阶级文化协会（Proletkul't，无产阶级文化人民委员部）的所有组织都“有无条件的义务把自己看作”教育人民委员部（Narkompros，教育人民委员部）各组织的“严格附属机构”（Arnol'dov et al. 1984, 171）。换言之，文化组织（一切理智、科学与艺术实践的形式）从属于教育与政治组织，一切形式的文化生产都要受到党的全面监督。该论证认为，正是这种附属地位，才能使这些组织为建设新社会发挥其全部创造潜力。", "苏联国家一方面不断焦虑于为国家对文化生产的控制公开辩护，另一方面又试图促进文化生产的独立性与实验性，这种持续的焦虑正是这一悖论的体现。迟至1984年，由莫斯科马克思列宁主义研究院的一批文化理论家集体撰写的《马克思列宁主义文化理论》（Marksistsko-leninskaia teoriia kul'tury）一书（Arnol'dov et al.），仍在为这一观点辩护。这本书开篇说，也许有人会认为，要在理智、科学与艺术领域的文化生产中真正做到富有创造性，这种工作就不能被控制和指挥。该书接着论证，尽管这种观点并非全然错误，但它只讲了问题的一个方面，忽视了所有文化生产不可化约的双重性。事实上，该书论证道，创造性工作始终既是创造者个人“严格意义上的私事”，又是一种“社会效用劳动”，在社会中创造着“精神价值”与“社会道德规范”。在社会主义社会中，文化生产的这两个方面被承认具有同等重要性，因为在这一社会里，“新人的形成不是自发的，而是自觉的，是有目的的教育工作的结果”。因此，在社会主义语境中，创造活动的独立性与党对创造性工作的控制并非相互矛盾，而必须同时加以追求（Arnol'dov et al. 1984, 162, 163）。这本书话语中引人注目的并非论证本身，而是这个想象中的争论在整个苏联历史中需要不断被重新提起，这暗示着社会主义核心处存在着持久的张力。", "这种张力并不局限于科学与艺术领域，而是关系到苏联社会中产生并流通的一切话语和知识形式。正如后续章节将表明的，在苏联历史的较早时期，政治、科学与艺术先锋派的响亮声音掩盖了这一悖论。他们将自己置于意识形态话语领域“之外”，从那个外在位置对这一话语公开发表评论并进行调整。革命后最初几年的特征是创造力与实验的爆发，但最终让位于对知识先锋派以及一切实验性文化与科学的压制，并引入了严格而统一的党的控制。22 这一转变之所以可能、并且显得合乎逻辑，正是因为革命工程自身的意识形态所固有的悖论。", "此时正是斯大林扮演了列斐伏尔所说的“主人”的角色：他立于意识形态话语之外，从那个外在位置对之进行编辑式的评点，从而通过他本人掩盖了这一悖论。这一外在位置使一种公共元话语得以产生并广泛流通，它针对一切政治、艺术与科学表达形式，依据一个外在的准则——马克思列宁主义教条——评判其是否精确、是否准确。斯大林相对于一切话语和知识形式的“外在”编辑位置，使他得以独一无二地接近那个用以评判它们的外在准则，这对那些成为其政权标志的现象的出现至关重要：他巨大的政治权力；他的个人崇拜；他亲自参与编辑政治讲话、科学论文、电影和音乐作品；在党组织中开展的清洗运动；以及最终导致数百万人丧生的大清洗。在斯大林统治的最后几年，尤其是1953年他去世以及随后对其个人崇拜的谴责之后，这个相对于话语和知识的外在位置消失了。这一发展的主要结果并非对某个具体领导人的谴责，而是对整个国家社会主义话语体制的重大重组：一个外在于意识形态（政治的、科学的、艺术的）话语、可据此发起关于该话语之元话语的位置不复存在，因此，关于意识形态的元话语从公共流通中消失了（关于这一过程的讨论见第2章）。", "既然不再有外在的声音能够掩盖苏联意识形态的列斐伏尔悖论，构成这一悖论的目标与手段之间的不协调便得以释放。这一变化最终在晚期社会主义时期导致苏联一切类型意识形态话语的结构（从意识形态的语言，到意识形态仪式、实践与组织的性质）发生深刻转变。由于这一转变，阅读意识形态表征时，把握其精确的结构形式，变得比解读其“字面”（指涉性）意义更为重要。话语体制的这一转变最终在晚期苏联文化内部引发了深刻的变迁：在严格程式化的意识形态形式、仪式与组织的语境中，打开了不确定性、创造性与意料之外意义的空间。就这样，列斐伏尔的悖论回来纠缠苏联体制。它促成了对社会主义体制深刻的内部重新阐释与置换，制造出一系列相互矛盾的条件，使该体制的崩溃在刚开始时显得如此出人意料，而一旦发生，又显得如此不令人意外、如此迅速。"]}

这一转变之所以可能、并且显得合乎逻辑，正是因为革命工程自身的意识形态所固有的悖论。", "此时正是斯大林扮演了列斐伏尔所说的“主人”的角色：他立于意识形态话语之外，从那个外在位置对之进行编辑式的评点，从而通过他本人掩盖了这一悖论。这一外在位置使一种公共元话语得以产生并广泛流通，它针对一切政治、艺术与科学表达形式，依据一个外在的准则——马克思列宁主义教条——评判其是否精确、是否准确。斯大林相对于一切话语和知识形式的“外在”编辑位置，使他得以独一无二地接近那个用以评判它们的外在准则，这对那些成为其政权标志的现象的出现至关重要：他巨大的政治权力；他的个人崇拜；他亲自参与编辑政治讲话、科学论文、电影和音乐作品；在党组织中开展的清洗运动；以及最终导致数百万人丧生的大清洗。在斯大林统治的最后几年，尤其是1953年他去世以及随后对其个人崇拜的谴责之后，这个相对于话语和知识的外在位置消失了。这一发展的主要结果并非对某个具体领导人的谴责，而是对整个国家社会主义话语体制的重大重组：一个外在于意识形态（政治的、科学的、艺术的）话语、可据此发起关于该话语之元话语的位置不复存在，因此，关于意识形态的元话语从公共流通中消失了（关于这一过程的讨论见第2章）。", 翻译时结合并遵守其他输入字段提供的信息。

{
  "sources": [
    "## Acts and Rituals",
    "During the late Soviet period, the form of ideological representations—documents, speeches, ritualized practices, slogans, posters, monuments, and urban visual propaganda— became increasingly normalized, ubiquitous, and predictable.",
    "This standardization of the form of discourse developed gradually, as a result of the disappearance, in the 1950s, of the external editorial voice that commented on that discourse. With that shift, the form of the ideological representations became fixed and replicated—unchanged from one context to the next. These representations no longer had to be read literally, at least in most contexts, to work perfectly well as elements of the hegemonic representation. This fixed and normalized discursive system was akin to the kind of discourse that Bakhtin terms “authoritative discourse” (avtoritetnoe slovo). For Bakhtin, authoritative discourse coheres around a strict external idea or dogma (whether religious, political, or otherwise) and occupies a particular position within the discursive regime of a period. It has two main features. First, because of a special “script” in which it is coded, authoritative discourse is sharply demarcated from all other types of discourse that coexist with it, which means that it does not depend on them, it precedes them, and it cannot be changed by them. Second, all these other types of discourse are organized around it. Their existence depends on being positioned in relation to it, having to refer to it, quote it, praise it, interpret it, apply it, and so forth, but they cannot, for example, interfere with its code and change it. Regardless of whether this demarcated and fixed authoritative discourse is successful in persuading its authors and audiences, they experience it as immutable and therefore unquestionable (Bakhtin 1994, 342–43).23 To stress that during late socialism the newly normalized Soviet ideological discourse no longer functioned at the level of meaning as a kind of ideology in the usual sense of the word, I will refer to it henceforth as “authoritative discourse.”",
    "The change in the functioning of Soviet ideology during late socialism was reflected in how Soviet citizens participated in ideological rituals and events, as described in many ethnographic accounts. For example, it is well known that during the period from the 1960s to the 1980s, the overwhelming majority of Soviet people participated in May Day and Revolution Day parades in Soviet cities. The apotheosis of such parades in the cities was the walk across the central square in front of the city’s party leaders, who stood on a high platform and waved to the marching masses. People cheered as oficial slogans blared from the loudspeakers, and the thundering roar of these hundreds of thousands of voices sounded impressive and unanimous. According to Soviet newspapers at the time, these massive events “convincingly demonstrate[d] the unbreakable union of the party and the people. . . .” (Pravda May 2, 1981). In practice, however, most people in the parades paid litle atention to the slogans, and many were not aware who exactly was depicted on the Politburo portraits they carried.",
    "Most Soviet citizens also regularly participated in various state elections for city or district government positions. These elections usually had a single oficial candidate and invariably produced a massive vote of support, though in practice the voters were relatively uninterested and/or ignorant as to who they were voting for. Sergei (born in 1962) remembers: “Usually I was not quite sure what type of elections these were, or who the candidate was. I would just go to the local election center, take the ballot with the candidate’s name, and put it in the voting box. This was the whole procedure for me. I would forget the name of the candidate a few minutes later. I don’t remember ever worrying that I was not more interested or that the elections were ‘fake.’” Most young people also regularly atended Komsomol (Communist Union of Youth) meetings at schools, colleges, factories, and other locations. At such meetings, it was not uncommon for people to participate in certain procedures without paying close attention to their literal meanings, such as voting in favor of resolutions without knowing what they said. This was not always the case, but it was certainly a dominant paradigm. Among small groups, the required Komsomol meetings were often reported without actually being held. Anna (born in 1961) remembers regular Komsomol meetings in her student group (twenty to twenty-five people) in college in the early 1980s, where “the komsorg (the meeting’s convener) would often suggest: ‘Maybe we should just write down that we had a discussion and voted in favor of the resolution, without actually having the discussion? I understand that everyone has things to atend to at home.’”",
    "What should we make of these acts of mass participation and support in which people regularly paid litle atention to the literal meanings of the ritualized acts and pronouncements in which they participated? Can these acts be described as pure masquerade and dissimulation, practiced in public for the gaze of the state and collective surveillance? This book argues that these acts cannot be reduced in this way, and instead ofers a dif­ erent interpretation. An examination of how these ritualized events and texts operated and what they meant to those enacting them is crucial to an understanding of the inherent paradoxes of late socialism. In most contexts these unanimous acts, gestures, and uterances of support did not refer to the literal meaning of ideological statements, resolutions, and figures, but rather performed a dif­ erent role. For this analysis, we need first to understand the discursive conditions under which authoritative discourse was produced, circulated, and received in late socialism."

function.arguments: {"targets": ["## 行为与仪式", "在晚期苏联时期，意识形态表征的形式——文件、讲话、仪式化的实践、口号、宣传画、纪念碑以及城市视觉宣传——日益变得规范化、无处不在且可预测。", "这种话语形式的标准化是逐渐发展起来的，其原因在于1950年代，那种对这一话语加以评论的外在编辑声音消失了。随着这一转变，意识形态表征的形式变得固定并被复制——从一种语境到另一种语境毫无变化。这些表征不再需要被字面阅读——至少在大多数语境中如此——就能作为霸权表征的元素完美地发挥作用。这种固定而规范化的话语系统，类似于巴赫金所称的“权威话语”（avtoritetnoe slovo）。在巴赫金看来，权威话语围绕某种严格的外在观念或教条（无论是宗教的、政治的还是其他性质的）凝聚而成，并在一个时期的话语体制中占据特定位置。它有两个主要特征。第一，由于它以某种特殊的“脚本”编码，权威话语与所有与之共存的其它类型话语截然区分开来，这意味着它不依赖于它们，先于它们存在，也不能被它们改变。第二，所有其它类型的话语都围绕它组织起来。它们的存在取决于被定位于与它的关系中，必须指涉它、引用它、赞美它、阐释它、运用它，如此等等，但它们不能，比如说，介入它的编码并改变它。无论这种被划界并固定的权威话语是否成功地说服了其作者和受众，他们都把它体验为不可改变的、因而是不可置疑的（Bakhtin 1994, 342–43）。23 为了强调在晚期社会主义时期，新近规范化的苏联意识形态话语不再在意义层面上作为通常意义上的意识形态发挥作用，我此后将把它称为“权威话语”。", "晚期社会主义时期苏联意识形态运作方式的变化，反映在苏联公民如何参与意识形态仪式与活动上，这一点在许多民族志记述中都有描述。例如，众所周知，在1960年代至1980年代期间，绝大多数苏联人都参加了苏联城市中的五一劳动节和革命节游行。此类城市游行的顶点，是走过中央广场、来到站在高台上向游行人群挥手致意的城市党委领导人面前。人们欢呼着，官方口号从扩音器中轰鸣传出，数十万人发出的雷鸣般的呐喊听起来气势磅礴、异口同声。据当时苏联报纸的报道，这些大规模活动“令人信服地证明了党与人民不可分割的团结……”（《真理报》1981年5月2日）。然而实际上，游行队伍中的大多数人并不留意那些口号，许多人也不知道自己举着的政治局画像上画的究竟是谁。", "大多数苏联公民还定期参加城市或区级政府职位的各类国家选举。这些选举通常只有一名官方候选人，并且总是产生压倒性的支持票，尽管实际上选民们相对不感兴趣，和/或不清楚自己在投票给谁。谢尔盖（生于1962年）回忆道：“我通常不太清楚这是什么类型的选举，也不知道候选人是谁。我只会去当地的选举站，拿上有候选人名字的选票，投进投票箱。对我来说，整个程序就到此为止。几分钟后我就会忘记候选人的名字。我不记得自己曾担心过为什么没有更感兴趣，或者选举是‘假的’。”大多数年轻人还定期在学校、学院、工厂及其他场所参加共青团（共产主义青年团）会议。在这种会议上，人们参与某些程序而不细究其字面含义，比如在不知道决议内容的情况下投票赞成决议，这并不罕见。这并非总是如此，但肯定是占主导地位的模式。在小团体中，按规定必须召开的共青团会议往往在没有实际召开的情况下被上报为已经召开。安娜（生于1961年）回忆道，1980年代初她在大学的学生小组（二十至二十五人）中定期召开的共青团会议上，“团组织委员（会议的召集人）常常提议：‘也许我们直接写上进行了讨论并投票赞成决议，而不真正进行讨论？我理解大家家里都有事要忙。’”", "我们该如何理解这些大众参与和拥护的行为——在这些行为中，人们经常不留意自己所参与的仪式化行为和宣告的字面含义？这些行为能否被描述为纯粹的假面舞会和伪饰，为了国家和集体监视的注视而在公共场合上演？本书认为，这些行为不能被如此化约，而是提出了另一种解释。考察这些仪式化的事件和文本如何运作、对实施它们的人意味着什么，对于理解晚期社会主义的内在悖论至关重要。在大多数语境中，这些异口同声的拥护行为、姿态和话语并不指涉意识形态陈述、决议和人物形象的字面含义，而是发挥了另一种作用。要进行这一分析，我们首先需要理解权威话语在晚期社会主义中得以生产、流通和被接受的话语条件。"]}

tool_calls.arguments: {"targets": ["## 行为与仪式", "在晚期苏联时期，意识形态表征的形式——文件、讲话、仪式化的实践、口号、宣传画、纪念碑以及城市视觉宣传——日益变得规范化、无处不在且可预测。", "这种话语形式的标准化是逐渐发展起来的，其原因在于1950年代，那种对这一话语加以评论的外在编辑声音消失了。随着这一转变，意识形态表征的形式变得固定并被复制——从一种语境到另一种语境毫无变化。这些表征不再需要被字面阅读——至少在大多数语境中如此——就能作为霸权表征的元素完美地发挥作用。这种固定而规范化的话语系统，类似于巴赫金所称的“权威话语”（avtoritetnoe slovo）。在巴赫金看来，权威话语围绕某种严格的外在观念或教条（无论是宗教的、政治的还是其他性质的）凝聚而成，并在一个时期的话语体制中占据特定位置。它有两个主要特征。第一，由于它以某种特殊的“脚本”编码，权威话语与所有与之共存的其它类型话语截然区分开来，这意味着它不依赖于它们，先于它们存在，也不能被它们改变。第二，所有其它类型的话语都围绕它组织起来。它们的存在取决于被定位于与它的关系中，必须指涉它、引用它、赞美它、阐释它、运用它，如此等等，但它们不能，比如说，介入它的编码并改变它。无论这种被划界并固定的权威话语是否成功地说服了其作者和受众，他们都把它体验为不可改变的、因而是不可置疑的（Bakhtin 1994, 342–43）。23 为了强调在晚期社会主义时期，新近规范化的苏联意识形态话语不再在意义层面上作为通常意义上的意识形态发挥作用，我此后将把它称为“权威话语”。", "晚期社会主义时期苏联意识形态运作方式的变化，反映在苏联公民如何参与意识形态仪式与活动上，这一点在许多民族志记述中都有描述。例如，众所周知，在1960年代至1980年代期间，绝大多数苏联人都参加了苏联城市中的五一劳动节和革命节游行。此类城市游行的顶点，是走过中央广场、来到站在高台上向游行人群挥手致意的城市党委领导人面前。人们欢呼着，官方口号从扩音器中轰鸣传出，数十万人发出的雷鸣般的呐喊听起来气势磅礴、异口同声。据当时苏联报纸的报道，这些大规模活动“令人信服地证明了党与人民不可分割的团结……”（《真理报》1981年5月2日）。然而实际上，游行队伍中的大多数人并不留意那些口号，许多人也不知道自己举着的政治局画像上画的究竟是谁。", "大多数苏联公民还定期参加城市或区级政府职位的各类国家选举。这些选举通常只有一名官方候选人，并且总是产生压倒性的支持票，尽管实际上选民们相对不感兴趣，和/或不清楚自己在投票给谁。谢尔盖（生于1962年）回忆道：“我通常不太清楚这是什么类型的选举，也不知道候选人是谁。我只会去当地的选举站，拿上有候选人名字的选票，投进投票箱。对我来说，整个程序就到此为止。几分钟后我就会忘记候选人的名字。我不记得自己曾担心过为什么没有更感兴趣，或者选举是‘假的’。”大多数年轻人还定期在学校、学院、工厂及其他场所参加共青团（共产主义青年团）会议。在这种会议上，人们参与某些程序而不细究其字面含义，比如在不知道决议内容的情况下投票赞成决议，这并不罕见。这并非总是如此，但肯定是占主导地位的模式。在小团体中，按规定必须召开的共青团会议往往在没有实际召开的情况下被上报为已经召开。安娜（生于1961年）回忆道，1980年代初她在大学的学生小组（二十至二十五人）中定期召开的共青团会议上，“团组织委员（会议的召集人）常常提议：‘也许我们直接写上进行了讨论并投票赞成决议，而不真正进行讨论？我理解大家家里都有事要忙。’”", "我们该如何理解这些大众参与和拥护的行为——在这些行为中，人们经常不留意自己所参与的仪式化行为和宣告的字面含义？这些行为能否被描述为纯粹的假面舞会和伪饰，为了国家和集体监视的注视而在公共场合上演？本书认为，这些行为不能被如此化约，而是提出了另一种解释。考察这些仪式化的事件和文本如何运作、对实施它们的人意味着什么，对于理解晚期社会主义的内在悖论至关重要。在大多数语境中，这些异口同声的拥护行为、姿态和话语并不指涉意识形态陈述、决议和人物形象的字面含义，而是发挥了另一种作用。要进行这一分析，我们首先需要理解权威话语在晚期社会主义中得以生产、流通和被接受的话语条件。"]}

{

    "## Actors in Masks",
    "One common atempt to explain how ideological texts and rituals function in contexts dominated by unchallengeable authoritative discourse whose meanings are not necessarily read literally is to assert that citizens act “as if ” they support these slogans and rituals in public, while privately believing something dif­ erent. Underlying this model are theories of mimicry and dissimulation. A recently influential approach to these theories can be found in the work of Peter Sloterdijk. In Critique of Cynical Reason Sloterdijk argues that in the contemporary West the success of ideology is based not on Marx’s classic formula of “false consciousness” (“they do not know it, but they are doing it”), but on what he calls “enlightened false consciousness” (“they know very well what they are doing, but still, they are doing it”). According to Sloterdijk, many Western subjects are postmodern cynics who insist on wearing a mask of misrecognition because they know that the ideology of the consumer society is unavoidable, even though they also know perfectly well that this ideology misrepresents social reality (Sloterdijk 1993; Žižek 1991a, 29). This model of acting “as if ” echoes James Scot’s (1990) discussion of the discourse of subaltern subjects that proceeds in two distinct transcripts, “official” and “hidden”—one representing a mask, the other the truth behind it. Lisa Wedeen, in a recent analysis of the “authoritarian” rule of President Asad in Syria, draws on Sloterdijk and Scot to argue that the art of publicly acting “as if ” they subscribed to ideological claims, without really believing them, allowed common citizens “to keep their actual thought private,” sustaining a “gap . . . between performance and belief ” (Wedeen 1999, 82). Slavoj Žižek (1991a) draws on a similar model of acting “as if ” to theorize the basis of power in Eastern European state socialism.",
    "In 1978, in the famous essay “The Power of the Powerless,” Václav Havel (1986) constructs a similar model of state socialism in the Eastern Europe of the 1970s. According to Havel, the citizens of socialist Czechoslovakia lived “in lies”: they acted in public as if they supported ideological slogans and messages even though privately they believed them to be false. This mode of conformism, argues Havel, allowed them to be left alone by the regime and to avoid personal problems—a reasoning Havel found morally reprehensible (1986, 49–51). In the Soviet Russian context, a related model has been developed by Oleg Kharkhordin. Kharkhordin argues that the subject of late Soviet society was a dissimulator who acted diferently in two dif­ erent spheres, the “oficial public” and the “hidden intimate.” According to that model the dissimulating subject was split: its hidden intimate self was only “available to the gaze of the closest friends or family members but sometimes kept secret even from them” (1999, 357), making it possible to spot these dissimulators only when they “suddenly let their strict self-control go and [broke] their utmost secrecy” (275).",
    "All these models share a crucial problem: although they provide an alternative to the binary division between the recognition and misrecognition of ideology, they do so by producing another problematic binary between “truth” and “falsity,” “reality” and “mask,” “revealing” and “dissimulating.” According to this binary model, such public political acts as voting in favor of an oficial resolution or displaying a pro-government slogan at a rally should be interpreted “literally”—as declarations of one’s support for the state that are either true (“real” support) or false (“dissimulation” of support).24 Several problematic assumptions about language, knowledge, meaning, and personhood lie at the basis of this understanding. In this view, the only function of language is to refer to the world and to state facts about it. That is why models based on such an understanding divide language into “codes,” such as oficial, or public, transcript and hidden, or intimate, transcript.25 Knowledge in this view exists before discourse. Discourse reflects knowledge and does not produce it. Meaning, accordingly, is a psychological state that is fully formed in the mind of the speaker before the act of speaking.26 The speaking person, in these models, is a unified, bounded, sovereign individual who possesses a “unique self-constituted” consciousness (Mitchell 1990, 545) and a “unitary speaking ego” (Hanks 2000, 182), and whose authentic voice can be hidden or revealed.27"

function.arguments: {"targets": ["## 面具下的行动者", "对于意识形态文本与仪式在由不容挑战的权威话语主导的语境中如何运作——在这样的语境里，这些话语的含义并不必然被照字面阅读——一种常见的解释是断言：公民在公开场合表现得“好像”支持这些口号与仪式，而私下里却相信着不同的东西。这一模式的基础是模仿（mimicry）与伪装（dissimulation）理论。对这一类理论，近年产生重要影响的阐述见于彼得·斯洛特戴克（Peter Sloterdijk）的著作。在《犬儒理性批判》（Critique of Cynical Reason）中，斯洛特戴克论证说，在当代西方，意识形态的成功所凭借的不是马克思的经典公式——“虚假意识”（“他们不知道，但他们正在这样做”）——而是他所称的“开明的虚假意识”（“他们非常清楚自己在做什么，但仍然照做不误”）。按照斯洛特戴克的说法，许多西方主体是后现代犬儒者，他们执意戴上一副误认（misrecognition）的面具，因为他们知道消费社会的意识形态不可避免，尽管他们同样清楚地知道，这种意识形态歪曲了社会现实（Sloterdijk 1993; Žižek 1991a, 29）。这种“好像”式行动模式，呼应了詹姆斯·斯科特（James Scot, 1990）对从属主体话语的讨论：这种话语以两种截然不同的“剧本”（transcripts）展开——“公开的”与“隐藏的”——其中一种代表面具，另一种代表面具背后的真相。丽莎·韦丁（Lisa Wedeen）在最近对叙利亚阿萨德总统“威权主义”统治的分析中，借鉴斯洛特戴克与斯科特，论证说：公开表演出“好像”信奉意识形态主张、而实际并不真正相信的艺术，使普通公民得以“将自己的真实想法保持为私密”，从而维系着“表演与信念之间的……裂隙”（Wedeen 1999, 82）。斯拉沃热·齐泽克（1991a）也借鉴了类似的“好像”式行动模式，用以对东欧国家社会主义中权力的基础进行理论化。", "1978年，瓦茨拉夫·哈维尔（Václav Havel）在著名的《无权者的权力》（“The Power of the Powerless”）一文中，为1970年代东欧的国家社会主义建构了类似的模式（Havel 1986）。按照哈维尔的说法，社会主义捷克斯洛伐克的公民“生活在谎言之中”：他们在公开场合表现得仿佛支持意识形态的口号与讯息，尽管私下里相信它们是虚假的。哈维尔论证说，这种从众模式使他们得以不被政权打扰，也得以避开个人麻烦——哈维尔认为这种推理在道德上应受谴责（1986, 49–51）。在苏联俄国的语境中，奥列格·哈尔霍尔金（Oleg Kharkhordin）发展了一种相关的模式。哈尔霍尔金论证说，晚期苏联社会的主体是一个伪装者（dissimulator），他在两个不同的领域——“官方公共”与“隐藏的亲密”——表现出不同的行为。按照这一模式，伪装的主体是分裂的：其隐藏的亲密自我只“向最亲近的朋友或家人敞开，但有时甚至对他们也保密”（1999, 357），因此人们只有当他们“突然放松严格的自我控制并[打破]其极端的保密”时（275），才有可能识破这些伪装者。", "所有这些模式都共有一个关键问题：尽管它们为意识形态的承认与误认之间的二元划分提供了替代方案，但它们这样做的方式，却是制造出另一组成问题的二元对立——“真实”与“虚假”、“现实”与“面具”、“显露”与“伪装”。按照这种二元模式，诸如投票赞成一份官方决议、或在集会上展示亲政府标语之类的公开政治行为，都应当被“照字面”理解——即被理解为对自己支持国家的声明，这种声明要么是真的（“真正的”支持），要么是假的（对支持的“伪装”）。²⁴ 在这一理解的基础上，潜藏着若干关于语言、知识、意义与人格的有问题的假设。按照这种观点，语言的唯一功能是指称世界、陈述关于世界的事实。正因如此，基于这种理解的模式把语言划分为各种“代码”，例如官方的或公开的剧本，以及隐藏的或亲密的剧本。²⁵ 在这种观点中，知识先于话语而存在。话语反映知识，而非生产知识。相应地，意义是一种心理状态，它在说话行为发生之前就已完整地形成于说话者的头脑之中。²⁶ 在这些模式中，说话的人是一个统一的、有边界的、自主的个体，他拥有“独特的自我构成”（unique self-constituted）的意识（Mitchell 1990, 545）和一个“统一的言说自我”（unitary speaking ego）（Hanks 2000, 182），其真实的声音可以被隐藏或显露。²⁷"]}

Let me also double-check "Lisa Wedeen" — 丽莎·韦丁. Yes, that's a common rendering. Some use 丽莎·韦迪恩. I'll use 韦丁.

"Peter Sloterdijk" — 彼得·斯洛特戴克. Common rendering: 斯洛特戴克 or 斯洛特迪杰克. I'll use 斯洛特戴克.

"Václav Havel" — 瓦茨拉夫·哈维尔. Yes.

"Oleg Kharkhordin" — 奥列格·哈尔霍尔金. Common: 哈尔霍丁 or 哈尔霍尔金. Kharkhordin is often rendered 哈尔霍尔金. I'll use that.

"Slavoj Žižek" — 斯拉沃热·齐泽克. Yes.

"James Scott" — 詹姆斯·斯科特. Yes.

Now, "Critique of Cynical Reason" — 《犬儒理性批判》. Yes.

"The Power of the Powerless" — 《无权者的权力》. Yes, standard translation.

Now let me write out the final targets and save.

Let me also reconsider sentence 1 phrasing once more. Original: "One common atempt to explain how ideological texts and rituals function in contexts dominated by unchallengeable authoritative discourse whose meanings are not necessarily read literally is to assert that citizens act 'as if' they support these slogans and rituals in public, while privately believing something different."

The relative clause "whose meanings are not necessarily read literally" modifies "authoritative discourse" — i.e., the meanings of the authoritative discourse are not necessarily read literally. My translation: "要解释意识形态文本与仪式在由不容挑战的权威话语主导的语境中如何运作——在这种语境中，这些含义并不必然被照字面阅读——一种常见的做法是断言……" Hmm, "这些含义" is a bit vague. Better: "——这种语境中的含义并不必然被照字面阅读——" or attach to 权威话语. Let me revise:

"要解释意识形态文本与仪式在由不容挑战的权威话语主导的语境中如何运作——在这种语境中，这些话语的含义并不必然被照字面理解——一种常见的做法是断言：公民在公开场合表现得"好像"支持这些口号与仪式，而私下里却相信着不同的东西。"

Hmm, "在这种语境中" repeats 语境. Alternatively:

"一种常见的做法是断言，公民在公开场合表现得"好像"支持这些口号与仪式，而私下里却相信着不同的东西——以此解释，意识形态文本与仪式在由不容挑战的权威话语所主导的语境中如何运作；在这种语境中，这些话语的含义并不必然被照字面阅读。"

That's more natural Chinese. Let me use this order.

Actually, let me keep it closer to the original structure while being readable:

"一种常见的做法是断言：公民在公开场合表现得"好像"支持这些口号与仪式，而私下里却相信着不同的东西——这一断言被用来解释，意识形态文本与仪式在由不容挑战的权威话语主导的语境中如何运作，而在此类语境中，这些话语的含义并不必然被照字面阅读。"

Hmm, getting convoluted. Let me simplify:

"对于意识形态文本与仪式在由不容挑战的权威话语主导的语境中如何运作——在这样的语境里，这些话语的含义并不必然被照字面阅读——一种常见的解释是断言：公民在公开场合表现得'好像'支持这些口号与仪式，而私下里却相信着不同的东西。"

Good. I'll go with that.

Let me finalize all four targets and save the draft, add glossary terms in parallel.

Glossary additions:
1. dissimulation → 伪装 (note: 与"显露"相对，本书本批核心概念)
2. dissimulator → 伪装者
3. misrecognition → 误认 (note: 与recognition相对)
4. enlightened false consciousness → 开明的虚假意识 (note: 斯洛特戴克/齐泽克用语)
5. public transcript → 公开剧本 (note: 斯科特《支配与抵抗的艺术》用语)
6. hidden transcript → 隐藏剧本

That's 6 terms. Good.

tool_calls.arguments: {"targets": ["## 面具下的行动者", "对于意识形态文本与仪式在由不容挑战的权威话语主导的语境中如何运作——在这样的语境里，这些话语的含义并不必然被照字面阅读——一种常见的解释是断言：公民在公开场合表现得“好像”支持这些口号与仪式，而私下里却相信着不同的东西。这一模式的基础是模仿（mimicry）与伪装（dissimulation）理论。对这一类理论，近年产生重要影响的阐述见于彼得·斯洛特戴克（Peter Sloterdijk）的著作。在《犬儒理性批判》（Critique of Cynical Reason）中，斯洛特戴克论证说，在当代西方，意识形态的成功所凭借的不是马克思的经典公式——“虚假意识”（“他们不知道，但他们正在这样做”）——而是他所称的“开明的虚假意识”（“他们非常清楚自己在做什么，但仍然照做不误”）。按照斯洛特戴克的说法，许多西方主体是后现代犬儒者，他们执意戴上一副误认（misrecognition）的面具，因为他们知道消费社会的意识形态不可避免，尽管他们同样清楚地知道，这种意识形态歪曲了社会现实（Sloterdijk 1993; Žižek 1991a, 29）。这种“好像”式行动模式，呼应了詹姆斯·斯科特（James Scot, 1990）对从属主体话语的讨论：这种话语以两种截然不同的“剧本”（transcripts）展开——“公开的”与“隐藏的”——其中一种代表面具，另一种代表面具背后的真相。丽莎·韦丁（Lisa Wedeen）在最近对叙利亚阿萨德总统“威权主义”统治的分析中，借鉴斯洛特戴克与斯科特，论证说：公开表演出“好像”信奉意识形态主张、而实际并不真正相信的艺术，使普通公民得以“将自己的真实想法保持为私密”，从而维系着“表演与信念之间的……裂隙”（Wedeen 1999, 82）。斯拉沃热·齐泽克（1991a）也借鉴了类似的“好像”式行动模式，用以对东欧国家社会主义中权力的基础进行理论化。", "1978年，瓦茨拉夫·哈维尔（Václav Havel）在著名的《无权者的权力》（“The Power of the Powerless”）一文中，为1970年代东欧的国家社会主义建构了类似的模式（Havel 1986）。按照哈维尔的说法，社会主义捷克斯洛伐克的公民“生活在谎言之中”：他们在公开场合表现得仿佛支持意识形态的口号与讯息，尽管私下里相信它们是虚假的。哈维尔论证说，这种从众模式使他们得以不被政权打扰，也得以避开个人麻烦——哈维尔认为这种推理在道德上应受谴责（1986, 49–51）。在苏联俄国的语境中，奥列格·哈尔霍尔金（Oleg Kharkhordin）发展了一种相关的模式。哈尔霍尔金论证说，晚期苏联社会的主体是一个伪装者（dissimulator），他在两个不同的领域——“官方公共”与“隐藏的亲密”——表现出不同的行为。按照这一模式，伪装的主体是分裂的：其隐藏的亲密自我只“向最亲近的朋友或家人敞开，但有时甚至对他们也保密”（1999, 357），因此人们只有当他们“突然放松严格的自我控制并[打破]其极端的保密”时（275），才有可能识破这些伪装者。", "所有这些模式都共有一个关键问题：尽管它们为意识形态的承认与误认之间的二元划分提供了替代方案，但它们这样做的方式，却是制造出另一组成问题的二元对立——“真实”与“虚假”、“现实”与“面具”、“显露”与“伪装”。按照这种二元模式，诸如投票赞成一份官方决议、或在集会上展示亲政府标语之类的公开政治行为，都应当被“照字面”理解——即被理解为对自己支持国家的声明，这种声明要么是真的（“真正的”支持），要么是假的（对支持的“伪装”）。²⁴ 在这一理解的基础上，潜藏着若干关于语言、知识、意义与人格的有问题的假设。按照这种观点，语言的唯一功能是指称世界、陈述关于世界的事实。正因如此，基于这种理解的模式把语言划分为各种“代码”，例如官方的或公开的剧本，以及隐藏的或亲密的剧本。²⁵ 在这种观点中，知识先于话语而存在。话语反映知识，而非生产知识。相应地，意义是一种心理状态，它在说话行为发生之前就已完整地形成于说话者的头脑之中。²⁶ 在这些模式中，说话的人是一个统一的、有边界的、自主的个体，他拥有“独特的自我构成”（unique self-constituted）的意识（Mitchell 1990, 545）和一个“统一的言说自我”（unitary speaking ego）（Hanks 2000, 182），其真实的声音可以被隐藏或显露。²⁷"]}

model_input.content:
你是翻译 Agent。
用户输入是一个翻译 batch，各字段含义如下：
- sources：本批需要翻译的原文列表；
- glossary_terms：翻译时应遵守的术语及固定译法；
- style：目标译文的风格要求；
- context：当前文本之前的局部上下文；
- book_synopsis：全书主题、背景和主线概览；
- chapter_digest：截至当前 batch 之前已经确认的累计章节梗概。

你的基本任务是翻译 sources 中的全部原文。输出译文是与 sources 等长的列表，按下标对应。
翻译时结合并遵守其他输入字段提供的信息。

{
  "sources": [
    "## The Performative",
    "In hopes of articulating a more nuanced understanding of late socialism and its paradoxes, we need to go beyond these problematic assumptions to examine how people living within that system engaged with, interpreted, and created their reality. The analysis in this book will consider discourse and forms of knowledge that circulated in everyday Soviet life not as divided into spheres or codes that are fixed and bounded, but as processes that are never completely known in advance and that are actively produced and reinterpreted (Haraway 1991, 190–91; Fabian 2001, 24).",
    "Many theories of language focus on its active and processual aspects. For example, Voloshinov stressed that the use of language involves a situated process in which meaning is produced, not simply reflected or communicated (Voloshinov 1986, 86).28 In his critique of the models of language that posit isolated bounded consciousness Bakhtin also pointed out that they ignore the ongoing and agentive processes constitutive of the event. Such models, he argued, can only transcribe an event as an accomplished static fact “at the cost of losing those actual creative forces which generated the event at the moment it was still being accomplished (when it was still open), i.e., at the cost of losing the living and in principle nonmerging participants in the event” (1990, 87). Instead, the productive and dialogic view of language developed by Bakhtin and his colleagues understands the speaking self as “voice” that is never bounded or static but always “dialogized,” because speaking implies inhabiting multiple voices that are not “self-enclosed or deaf to one another” but that “hear each other constantly, call back and forth to each other, and are reflected in one another” (1984, 75).29",
    "The productive nature of language is also central to John Austin’s analysis of “performatives” and the traditions in the study of language that are related to this approach (1999). Introducing speech act theory, Austin argues that in addition to “constative” uterances that state something (present facts or describe reality, such as “it is cold,” “my name is Joe”), language includes a whole class of uterances that do something. Such uterances as “Guilty!” (utered by a judge in a courtroom), “I name this ship the Queen Elizabeth” (at an oficial launching ceremony), or “I bet you sixpence it will rain tomorrow” perform an action that changes things in social reality instead of describing that reality. Austin calls this class of uterances “performative uterances” or “performatives.” Constative uterances convey meaning and can be true or false; performative uterances deliver force and cannot be true or false—instead they can be felicitous or infelicitous.",
    "Austin points out that what makes an uterance a performative is not the intention of the speaker, but rather the accepted conventions surrounding the uterance, which involve the appropriate person utering the appropriate words in the appropriate circumstances in order to obtain conventional results. If the conventions are not in place, the performative will not succeed regardless of the intention of the speaker (1999, 12–18). Conversely, if the conventions are in place, the performative will succeed regardless of intention. The issue of intention is central here, in light of our critical assessment of the abovementioned models that posit meaning in discourse as a psychological state that preexists the act of speaking. For example, speech acts such as oaths do not have to be intended, as a psychological state, to be performed. If a person makes an oath in court to tell the truth, though internally planning to conceal the truth, this does not make the execution of the oath any less real or eficacious, nor does it exonerate the person from legal repercussions if the lie is discovered. In other words, the very binding of this speech act within the system of laws, rules, or conventions (making it a recognized oath with consequences) does not depend on whether the speaker intended the words utered during the oath “for real” or “as if.”30",
    "In a critical reading of speech act theory Derrida pushed further Austin’s point that it is the conventions of a speech act, and not the intention of the speaker, that make a performative successful. The conventionality of a speech act implies that it must be formulated according to a recognized “coded” or “iterable” model—that is, it must function as a citation that is repeatable in an endless number of contexts (Derrida 1977, 191–92). However, the exhaustive knowledge of context cannot be achieved because any context is open to broader description and because contexts in which new citations of the same speech act can appear are potentially infinite (Derrida 1977, 185–86). Because of the citationality of a speech act and the indeterminacy of context, the meaning of any given speech act is never completely determined in advance. Each speech act can break with context in unpredictable ways and achieve efects and mean things that were not intended in advance. This ability of the speech act to break with context, argues Derrida, is a constitutive element of its performative force.31 By stressing the structural ability of a conventional formula to be used in unanticipated ways,",
    "Derrida’s argument recognizes the possibility for change and unpredictability even within strictly controlled and reproduced norms and conventions. At the same time, by limiting the discussion to the semiotic level of discourse, Derrida downplays the role that external social conventions, institutions, and power relations also play in constituting the performative force of a conventional uterance.",
    "In a different critical reading of performative acts, Pierre Bourdieu (1991) focused precisely on that external dimension, adding a sociological analysis of Austin’s “conventions” that are necessary for a successful performance of speech acts. Bourdieu argues that the source of power of conventional speech acts “resides in the institutional conditions of their production and reception” (111) and that their power is “nothing other than the delegated power of the spokesperson” (107). Although Bourdieu’s focus provides a necessary external perspective on the social and institutional nature of power and the process of its delegation, it still privileges just one side of the performative: it downplays the role of the semiotic nature of discourse in constituting the performative force and consequently downplays the possibility for change in discourse that institutions cannot determine or anticipate in advance.",
    "A synthesis of Derrida’s and Bourdieu’s critical readings of Austin’s theory would allow one to consider both constitutive elements of the performative force of a speech act—the delegated power of external social contexts and institutions and the semiotic power of discourse to produce unpredictable meanings and efects in new contexts. It is precisely because the two elements of the performative force—sociological and semiotic— operate simultaneously that speech acts even in strictly controlled institutionalized contexts can take on meanings and produce effects for which they were not intended. This possibility of an unanticipated outcome constitutes, Judith Butler argues, “the political promise of the performative, one that positions the performative at the center of a political hegemony” (Butler 1997b, 161). This point is crucial for the following discussion of ideological rituals and uterances and the efects they produce."

4. "语言的生产性也是约翰·奥斯汀对"述行语"的分析以及与此路径相关的语言研究传统的核心（1999）。在引入言语行为理论时，奥斯汀论证道，除了陈述某事（呈现事实或描述现实，如"天很冷""我叫乔"）的"记述性"话语之外，语言还包括整整一类有所作为的话语。诸如"有罪！"（由法官在法庭上说出）、"我把这艘船命名为伊丽莎白女王号"（在官方下水仪式上）、"我赌六便士明天会下雨"这类话语，所实施的是改变社会现实中事物的行动，而非描述那种现实。奥斯汀称这类话语为"述行性话语"或"述行语"。记述性话语传达意义，可以为真或为假；述行性话语传递效力，无法为真或为假——相反，它们可以是适切的或不适切的。"

5. "奥斯汀指出，使一个话语成为述行语的，不是说话者的意图，而是围绕该话语的、已被接受的惯例，这些惯例涉及在适当的情境中由适当的人说出适当的言辞，以获得惯例性的结果。如果惯例不成立，那么无论说话者意图如何，述行语都不会成功（1999, 12–18）。反之，如果惯例成立，则无论意图如何，述行语都会成功。鉴于我们上文对上述种种模式的批判性评估——那些模式把话语中的意义预设为一种先于言说行为而存在的心理状态——意图问题在此处于核心地位。例如，誓言这类言语行为，并不需要作为一种心理状态被"有意为之"才能实施。如果一个人在法庭上宣誓说真话，尽管内心打算隐瞒真相，这并不会使誓言的履行变得不那么真实或有效，也不会在谎言被揭穿时使此人免于法律后果。换言之，这一言语行为被约束在法律、规则或惯例体系之内（使之成为具有后果的、被承认的誓言）这一事实本身，并不取决于说话者在宣誓时说出那些话究竟是"当真"还是"装作"。30"

6. "在对言语行为理论的批判性解读中，德里达进一步推进了奥斯汀的观点：使述行语成功的，是言语行为的惯例，而非说话者的意图。言语行为的惯例性意味着，它必须按照某种被承认的"编码化"或"可重复"的模式来表述——也就是说，它必须像一个能够在无数情境中不断重复的引文那样运作（Derrida 1977, 191–92）。然而，对情境的穷尽性认识是不可能实现的，因为任何情境都向更宽泛的描述开放，也因为同一言语行为的新引文可能出现的情境是潜在无限的（Derrida 1977, 185–86）。由于言语行为的引文性以及情境的不确定性，任何特定言语行为的意义都绝不会被事先完全确定。每个言语行为都能以不可预见的方式脱离情境，产生事先并未意图的效果、表达事先并未意图的意义。德里达论证道，言语行为这种脱离情境的能力，正是其述行性力量的构成要素。31 通过强调一个惯例性公式得以被以不可预期的方式使用的结构性能力，"

7. "德里达的论证承认，即使在受到严格控制和不断复制的规范与惯例内部，也存在变化与不可预测性的可能。与此同时，由于把讨论局限于话语的符号学层面，德里达淡化了外部的社会惯例、制度与权力关系在构成一个惯例性话语的述行性力量方面所起的作用。"

8. "在对述行行为的另一种批判性解读中，皮埃尔·布迪厄（1991）恰恰聚焦于这一外部维度，为奥斯汀所说的、成功实施言语行为所必需的"惯例"补充了一种社会学分析。布迪厄论证道，惯例性言语行为的力量之源"存在于其生产与接受的制度条件之中"（111），其力量"不过是代言人的被委派权力"（107）。尽管布迪厄的着眼点提供了看待权力的社会性与制度性本质及其委派过程的必要外部视角，它仍然只偏重述行性的一面：它淡化了话语的符号学性质在构成述行性力量方面的作用，因而也淡化了话语中那种制度无法事先决定或预见的变化的可能。"

9. "综合德里达与布迪厄对奥斯汀理论的批判性解读，将使我们得以同时考察一个言语行为的述行性力量的两个构成要素——外部社会情境与制度的被委派权力，以及话语在新的情境中产生不可预知的意义与效果的符号学力量。正因述行性力量的这两个要素——社会学要素与符号学要素——同时运作，言语行为即使在受到严格控制的制度化情境中，也能够承载并非为其而设的意义、产生并非为其而设的效果。朱迪斯·巴特勒论证道，这种意外结果的可能性构成了"述行性的政治承诺，它把述行性置于政治霸权的中心"（Butler 1997b, 161）。这一点对于下文讨论意识形态仪式与话语及其所产生的效果至关重要。"

"在对言语行为理论的批判性解读中，德里达进一步推进了奥斯汀的观点：使述行语成功的，是言语行为的惯例，而非说话者的意图。言语行为的惯例性意味着，它必须按照某种被承认的“编码化”或“可重复”的模式来表述——也就是说，它必须像一个能够在无数情境中不断重复的引文那样运作（Derrida 1977, 191–92）。然而，对情境的穷尽性认识是不可能实现的，因为任何情境都向更宽泛的描述开放，也因为同一言语行为的新引文可能出现的情境是潜在无限的（Derrida 1977, 185–86）。由于言语行为的引文性以及情境的不确定性，任何特定言语行为的意义都绝不会被事先完全确定。每个言语行为都能以不可预见的方式脱离情境，产生事先并未意图的效果、表达事先并未意图的意义。德里达论证道，言语行为这种脱离情境的能力，正是其述行性力量的构成要素。31 通过强调一个惯例性公式得以被以不可预期的方式使用的结构性能力，", "德里达的论证承认，即使在受到严格控制和不断复制的规范与惯例内部，也存在变化与不可预测性的可能。与此同时，由于把讨论局限于话语的符号学层面，德里达淡化了外部的社会惯例、制度与权力关系在构成一个惯例性话语的述行性力量方面所起的作用。", "在对述行行为的另一种批判性解读中，皮埃尔·布迪厄（1991）恰恰聚焦于这一外部维度，为奥斯汀所说的、成功实施言语行为所必需的“惯例”补充了一种社会学分析。布迪厄论证道，惯例性言语行为的力量之源“存在于其生产与接受的制度条件之中”（111），其力量“不过是代言人的被委派权力”（107）。尽管布迪厄的着眼点提供了看待权力的社会性与制度性本质及其委派过程的必要外部视角，它仍然只偏重述行性的一面：它淡化了话语的符号学性质在构成述行性力量方面的作用，因而也淡化了话语中那种制度无法事先决定或预见的变化的可能。", "综合德里达与布迪厄对奥斯汀理论的批判性解读，将使我们得以同时考察一个言语行为的述行性力量的两个构成要素——外部社会情境与制度的被委派权力，以及话语在新的情境中产生不可预知的意义与效果的符号学力量。正因述行性力量的这两个要素——社会学要素与符号学要素——同时运作，言语行为即使在受到严格控制的制度化情境中，也能够承载并非为其而设的意义、产生并非为其而设的效果。朱迪斯·巴特勒论证道，这种意外结果的可能性构成了“述行性的政治承诺，它把述行性置于政治霸权的中心”（Butler 1997b, 161）。这一点对于下文讨论意识形态仪式与话语及其所产生的效果至关重要。"]}
